lessons.title: The exchange is a company, not the blockchain
lessons.content:
# The exchange is a company, not the blockchain

Most people meet crypto through an **exchange**, not through a seed phrase. That is normal. It is also where a lot of confusion starts, because the screen looks like a wallet and is not one.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say, in your own words, what you actually own when a balance sits on Binance — an example of a centralised exchange, not “the only real one” — or on any similar platform, and what you do **not** own yet. The first heavy word is **exchange**: a company that keeps its own ledger of who is owed what, matches buyers and sellers, and sometimes sends coins on a public chain when you ask it to withdraw.

## Four objects, with a company in the middle

In the wallets course you named four objects: app, device lock, keys, chain. On an exchange the picture is different. Smash them together and you will later swear “the blockchain stole my money” when a company froze a row in a database.

**1. The website or app**

The branded product. It can be cloned. Bookmark the official domain the same way you bookmark a bank. Do not arrive through a sponsored ad, a Telegram button, or a “login to claim” SMS. The app is a company product. Products have outages, updates, and fake twins.

**2. Your account**

Email plus password plus whatever extra lock you add. This is a **login**, not a seed. Resetting a password is possible. That is a feature of a company. It is also a door for SIM-swap and email-takeover attacks. If you lose the login, you write to support. If you lose a seed, there is no support. Different objects.

**3. The company’s ledger**

The number you see — “12 USDT”, “0.02 BNB” — is a row in **their** database. They owe you, under their terms. They can freeze a withdrawal. They can halt a ticker. They can get hacked. The row is an **IOU**: an “I owe you,” a promise recorded in their book, not a coin sitting in an address whose keys you hold.

**4. The chain**

The public book — BNB Smart Chain, Ethereum, Tron, and the rest. You only touch it when you **deposit** (send from a wallet into their address) or **withdraw** (they send from their address to yours). Until then, you are not on-chain. BscScan will not show your name. It has never heard of your email.

TABLE
Object | What it is | If it fails
Exchange app | A company product | Phishing clone, outage, fake APK
Account login | Identity the company recognises | Password reset theft, 2FA loss
Exchange balance | An IOU in their ledger | Freeze, insolvency, ticker halt
On-chain coins | Entries on BNB Smart Chain or another book | Only after a completed withdrawal
ENDTABLE

## Why this design exists

Exchanges exist because a public chain does not take local currency from a GTBank app, dollars from a card, or euros from a SEPA transfer. Someone has to:

- collect local currency through banks, cards, or other people
- keep an **order book** so a buyer and a seller can meet
- hold inventory of crypto
- send you coins when you withdraw, after their risk team says yes

That someone is a **business**. Businesses have licenses in some countries, grey areas in others, terms of service, support tickets, and failure modes. Treating an exchange like “the blockchain” is how people are shocked when a withdrawal is delayed for compliance, or when a company pauses a ticker, or when a hack empties a hot wallet and customers wait in a queue of creditors.

A bank is also a company with a ledger. You already live with that. The new skill is seeing the same shape in a crypto app that uses the word “wallet” on a button.

**Worked scenario.** Jordan buys 50 USDT on an exchange using local currency. The app shows 50 USDT. He tells a group “I now hold USDT on BNB Smart Chain.” He does not — not yet.

1. His local currency left his bank and arrived, through P2P or a deposit corridor, as a credit on the exchange.
2. The exchange’s internal book says they owe him 50 USDT.
3. There is no BscScan row with his personal address.
4. Self-custody starts when a **withdrawal** lands on an address whose keys he holds.
5. Until that row exists on the chain he chose, he has a company promise, not a coin.

If the company is honest and online, the promise is useful. If the company is frozen, insolvent, or phished through his login, the promise is a support ticket.

DIAGRAM
Naira / local currency (bank, card, or P2P)
        |
        v
Exchange account (THEIR ledger — you have a login)
        |
        |  withdraw, with the RIGHT network selected
        v
Your wallet address on a chain (YOU have keys)
        |
        v
Public explorer (BscScan on BNB Smart Chain) shows the row
ENDDIAGRAM

## Named examples are examples, not a shopping list

This course will name Binance, Trust Wallet, BscScan, USDT, BNB, and Crystal Stones because students will meet those words. Naming them is not an endorsement and not an instruction to open an account today. If a platform is banned, slow, or untrusted in your country, the **ideas** still apply: company ledger, pair, fee, network, test send.

Crystal Stones, as a BEP-20 token on BNB Smart Chain, may or may not appear on any given exchange. Listing is a business decision. It is not proof of quality. You will learn to buy **practice** amounts of widely used assets — usually USDT and a little BNB for gas — so you can later move value on BNB Smart Chain. That is a skills path. It is not “buy Crystal Stones on this page.”

The public contract, to **verify** only, never as a buy order, is:

0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00

If a chat pastes a different address with the same name, it is a different object.

## What “the exchange got hacked” actually means

When a CEX is hacked, the thief usually stole keys to **the company’s** hot wallet, not your seed — you never had a seed on that platform. Customer balances are rows. The company must decide, under law and their terms, who they still owe. That can take months. Insurance, if any, is their product, not a law of the chain.

This is why “not your keys, not your coins” is a slogan with a precise meaning: until withdrawal, you are a customer, not a key-holder. The slogan does not mean “never use an exchange.” It means know which layer you are on.

NOTE
Academy staff will never DM you a “special deposit address” for tuition or a listing. Intermediate and Advanced tuition, when you reach it, goes through the academy’s published checkout: the checkout processor, paid in USDT on BEP-20. Not Crystal Stone token. Not PaynovaX. Not a wallet pasted in WhatsApp. An exchange login is not a seed, and nobody here will ask for either.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You are here so that “I have 50 USDT on the app” stops meaning “I have 50 USDT on BNB Smart Chain.” Those sentences describe two books. Mixing them is how people panic, get recovered by thieves, and blame the wrong layer.

## Say this out loud

- An exchange is a company with its own ledger, not the blockchain.
- An exchange balance is an IOU until a withdrawal confirms on-chain.
- The app is not the chain. The login is not a seed.
- Deposit and withdraw are the moments you actually touch a public book.
- Naming a platform is not a buy order, and Crystal Stones is not on this page as a shopping list.

Next: the two big families — centralized and decentralized — and why beginners almost always start on a CEX.

lessons.title: CEX versus DEX, without slogans
lessons.content:
# CEX versus DEX, without slogans

People argue “CEX bad, DEX freedom.” That argument skips the job each one does. You need both words, defined, before you pick a door with local currency in your pocket.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what a **CEX** is, what a **DEX** is, why someone with only local currency usually needs a CEX first, and why “Connect Wallet” is not automatically safer. PancakeSwap will be mentioned only as a DEX you are not using yet.

## CEX — centralized exchange

A **CEX** is a company. You create an account. You usually pass **KYC** (Know Your Customer — they record who you are). You send local currency or a card payment, or you use **P2P** (peer-to-peer: another user pays your bank, the company releases crypto). You trade on **their** matching engine. You withdraw when they allow it.

Binance is an example of a centralised exchange. So are many others. This course is not an advert for any of them. The shape is what you need: company, account, IOU, optional on-chain send later.

Strengths for a beginner:

- a door for local currency (bank, card, or P2P)
- password reset exists
- customer support exists (slowly)
- you can practise buying without holding a seed yet
- liquid pairs so a tiny market buy is usually boring

Costs:

- they can freeze you
- a phishing site can steal the login
- if the company fails, you are a creditor
- you are not in self-custody until withdrawal
- they can halt a ticker or pause withdrawals during chaos

None of that makes a CEX “fake crypto.” It makes it a **custodian**: they hold the keys to the coins that back (or are supposed to back) the IOUs on their screen.

## DEX — decentralized exchange

A **DEX** is software on a chain. Uniswap on Ethereum is one family. PancakeSwap on BNB Smart Chain is a DEX you are not using yet. There is no account in the CEX sense. You **connect a wallet**. You swap token A for token B by signing a transaction. The pool is a **smart contract** — a program on the chain that holds liquidity and follows published rules.

Strengths:

- no company signup for the swap itself
- you already had to have coins on that chain
- the trade settles on-chain; you can look up the hash

Costs:

- you need a wallet and gas (BNB on BSC)
- a fake DEX domain will drain you
- **approvals** can be unlimited (the Safety course covers this in full)
- no help desk if you sign the wrong thing
- price impact on thin pools can wreck a small trade
- it generally cannot collect local currency

A DEX does not “know your name.” That is not a moral halo. It also means the contract will not parent you.

TABLE
Question | CEX | DEX
Who holds keys during the trade? | The company | You
How do you get local currency in? | Bank, card, P2P | You generally cannot; you arrive with crypto
Can they freeze you? | Yes | The contract will not “know you”; scams still can empty you
Beginner first buy of USDT with local money? | This is the usual door | Usually the wrong door
Where is the receipt? | Their order history | A transaction hash on an explorer
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Amaka hears “just swap on PancakeSwap, KYC is slavery.” She has only local currency in a bank.

1. PancakeSwap cannot collect that local currency. There is no “pay with GTBank” button on the chain.
2. She would still need a CEX, a P2P seller, or some other on-ramp first.
3. Even after she had USDT on-chain, she would need BNB for gas to swap.
4. The slogan skipped the plumbing. She has not failed. The advice failed.
5. When she later meets a DEX in Intermediate, she will already know she is signing away tokens from a wallet she controls — a different risk than a CEX login.

DIAGRAM
Local currency (local currency, dollars, euros, ...)
        |
        v
CEX / on-ramp (company ledger)
        |
        |  withdraw to an address you control
        v
Wallet on a chain (keys + gas)
        |
        v
DEX / dApp later
(a DEX you are not using yet — needs coins + gas already on-chain)
ENDDIAGRAM

## Hybrid screens that pretend to be both

Some exchange apps show a swap button that is actually their internal ledger. Some open a browser into a DEX. Read which one you are in.

If there is no on-chain transaction hash you can paste into BscScan, you did not use a DEX. You used a company. That is allowed. It is not “decentralized” because the button said Swap.

Some wallets offer a “buy crypto” button that opens a third-party on-ramp. That third party is another company: KYC, fees, delays. The wallet did not become a bank. It linked one.

## Order of operations in this academy

1. Learn the CEX as a tool (this course).
2. Withdraw a **practice** amount to a wallet you control — only after the Wallets course habits are in your hands, not in a group chat.
3. Later courses treat DEX, liquidity, and token listings as a separate skill. You will not skip to a PancakeSwap ticker because a group called it “the Crystal Stones pool.”

A DEX listing is not a blessing. Anyone can create a BEP-20 and add a pool with a similar name. Verifying the Crystal Stones contract `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BscScan is the adult check. A pancake UI screenshot is not. This academy will not tell you to buy that token, on a CEX or a DEX.

## Custody is a sliding scale, not a personality

You can:

- keep practice size on a CEX while you learn
- withdraw what you intend to hold yourself
- leave nothing on an exchange you do not have a reason to leave

“Not your keys” is a layer description, not a purity contest. Adults use companies and self-custody for different jobs, the same way they use banks and cash.

NOTE
A DEX you are not using yet is still a thing you must be able to name, so a group cannot shame you into connecting a wallet this week. Connect Wallet on a DEX is not “safer by default.” It is a different risk: you can lose coins with one signature and no ticket number.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You should now be able to look at a screen and say “this is a company IOU” or “this is a wallet signature,” and refuse slogans that skip the on-ramp.

## Say this out loud

- CEX means company, account, on-ramp, IOU until withdraw.
- DEX means on-chain program, wallet signature, no local currency door.
- Beginners usually need a CEX first because they start with local currency.
- Connect Wallet on a DEX is not safer by default. It is a different risk.
- PancakeSwap is a DEX you are not using yet — not this course’s first buy.

Next: what you are actually looking at when the screen says BNB/USDT.

lessons.title: Spot, pairs, and what a price is
lessons.content:
# Spot, pairs, and what a price is

An exchange does not sell “crypto” as one product. It sells **pairs**. If you cannot read a pair, you cannot know what you paid.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to open a spot screen, name the base and the quote, say what bid, ask, last, and spread mean, and refuse the sentence “the price is X” as if the world had one official number. A **spot** market means: you buy or sell the asset now, for settlement on that platform’s books, not a bet on future price with borrowed money.

## Spot is now. Leverage is a different sport

**Spot** = you pay with money you have on the platform, you receive a book-entry of the asset. If you buy 0.01 BNB with USDT, your USDT IOU shrinks and your BNB IOU grows, after fees.

**Futures, margin, “100x,” perpetuals** are how beginners donate money to the house. They are bets with leverage: borrowed size, liquidations, funding rates. This course is **spot only**. We name the other buttons so you can walk past them. An academy that hides the casino floor is how students fall in.

If a screen offers “cross,” “isolated,” “leverage,” or “futures,” you are not in the lesson you think you are in. Leave.

## A pair is a price tag in another asset

**BNB/USDT** means: the price of one BNB, measured in USDT.

If the last trade was 600, one BNB cost 600 USDT **on that exchange, at that second**. Another exchange can show 599. A DEX pool can show 603. There is no single official world price. There are **venues**.

**Base** is the thing being priced (BNB). **Quote** is the measuring stick (USDT).

If you have local currency and you want USDT, you are looking for a **USDT/NGN** (or NGN/USDT) door, or a P2P advert priced in local currency — not a BNB chart. In other countries the quote might be USD, EUR, GBP, or a local currency the venue lists. Same idea: read both sides of the pair.

TABLE
Pair | You are buying or selling | You are paying or receiving
BNB/USDT | BNB | USDT
ETH/USDT | ETH | USDT
USDT/NGN | USDT | Naira (on venues that list NGN)
BTC/USDT | BTC | USDT
A random TOKEN/USDT | That token | USDT — only if you meant to
ENDTABLE

## Bid, ask, last, and the spread

The **bid** is what buyers are currently offering. The **ask** (or offer) is what sellers want. The **last** is the last trade that already happened. Last is history. It is not a promise that you can trade there now.

The **spread** is the gap between bid and ask. On a busy USDT pair the spread is tiny. On a thin token the spread is a trap: you “buy at 1.00” and can only sell at 0.92 immediately. That is not “the market crashed.” That is you paying the spread.

A **candle** is a picture of trades at one venue over a time bucket: open, high, low, close. It is not prophecy. This academy will not teach you to read candlesticks as a fortune. A screenshot of a green candle is a screenshot.

**Worked scenario.** A group screenshot shows Crystal Stones “pumping 40%.”

1. The screenshot is a 1-minute candle on a low-liquidity pair, possibly on a DEX you are not using yet.
2. The ask is one size. The bid is another. The last trade was a tiny print.
3. A market buy of a few hundred dollars would move the price against the buyer. That move is **price impact**, not a gift.
4. The chart lied by omission. Liquidity is part of the price.
5. Even if the ticker text says Crystal Stones, the contract on BNB Smart Chain must match `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` or it is a different object. This academy still will not tell you to buy it.

DIAGRAM
What the chart shows : last trade in a pair at one venue
What you pay         : last + spread + taker fee + later withdrawal fee
What you hold after  : a book-entry (CEX) or a token (DEX)

Price on a screenshot  is not  money in your control
ENDDIAGRAM

## Tickers are not contracts

Many tokens reuse names. “USDT” on that exchange might be:

- a book-entry the exchange calls USDT, redeemable as several on-chain flavours when you withdraw
- or a specific network’s USDT once you pick a withdrawal network

“Crystal Stones” on a random DEX is **not** automatically the project contract. Always match the address on BNB Smart Chain. If the ticker text matches and the contract does not, it is a different object. Logos are cheap. Contracts are the name.

The same warning applies to “BNB.” On a CEX, BNB is usually their IOU for the native coin of BNB Smart Chain. On a random chain, a token named BNB can be a toy. Read the network.

## What a price is, said slowly

A price is **the last agreed exchange rate on that venue, for that pair, at that moment, for the size that actually traded.** It is not:

- the number on a paid Telegram channel
- the number on CoinMarketCap delayed by minutes
- the number you wish you had clicked
- a guarantee you can enter or exit there with your size

When people say “the market,” they usually mean a soup of venues. Your fill happens on one of them.

NOTE
This academy will not teach you to read candlesticks as prophecy. A candle is a history of trades at one venue. It is not a promise. Education only — not a buy order for BNB, USDT, Crystal Stones, or anything else.
ENDNOTE

## Venue price is not oracle price

Some apps show a “global” price pulled from a data company. That number can be useful as a glance. It is not the price you will get on the pair you are about to click. The fill happens on **this** venue’s book, plus **this** venue’s fee.

If a widget says USDT is 1.000 and your P2P seller wants a higher quote local currency, you are not being cheated by mathematics. You are looking at two markets: a dollar-ish token on international venues, and a local local currency door with its own spread. Speak both numbers. Do not average them in your head and call the difference theft.

When Crystal Stones appears as a widget somewhere, the same rule applies: a displayed number is not a bid you can exit on, and this academy is still not telling you to buy it.

## What this lesson is for

You should now be able to look at a pair, name both sides, and treat “the price” as a venue fact plus spread plus fees — not a global truth.

## Say this out loud

- Spot means now, with money you have. Leverage is a later, optional, dangerous topic — not this course.
- A pair prices one asset in another. Read both sides.
- Bid, ask, last, and spread are different numbers. Last is history.
- Ticker text is not a contract address.
- A screenshot of a candle is not money in your control.

Next: fees, so “I bought at the chart price” stops being a sentence you use.

lessons.title: Fees, spread, and the price you actually paid
lessons.content:
# Fees, spread, and the price you actually paid

Beginners compare chart prices and ignore the bill. The bill has several lines. Miss one and you think the exchange “stole” 2 USDT.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name every line that sits between dollars, euros, or other local currency in a bank and coins you can actually move, and you should refuse the sentence “I bought at the chart price.” The heavy word is **all-in price**: what left your life, minus what you still control, including spread, trading fee, withdrawal fee, and later gas.

## The fee stack on a CEX

**1. Deposit / P2P / card cost**

Your bank may charge. A card corridor may charge. A P2P seller’s local currency price already includes **their** spread. If USDT is a local-currency quote on a blog and your seller wants a higher quote, the gap is a fee by another name. In a country with bank transfers or cards into an exchange, the corridor itself has FX markup, weekend delays, and sometimes a percentage. Same idea, different plumbing.

**2. Trading fee**

**Maker** and **taker**. A **taker** hits a resting order (a market buy is usually taker). A **maker** rests an order on the book. Beginners using market buttons pay taker fees. It is a percentage of the trade. Small, until you trade often. VIP schedules, BNB discounts, and coupon weeks are marketing. Learn the line on **your** receipt first.

**3. Spread**

Covered last lesson. On liquid USDT pairs, small. On exotic tokens, large. Spread is not printed as “fee” on some screens. It still left your pocket.

**4. Withdrawal fee**

A flat or percentage charge when coins leave the company to a chain. For USDT on BNB Smart Chain this is often modest. For USDT on Ethereum it can be ugly because **gas** is expensive and the exchange prices that in. This is one reason this academy standardises thinking on **BEP-20 / BNB Smart Chain** for practice — not because other networks are fake, because the fee behaviour is more beginner-survivable.

**5. Network gas after you leave**

Once USDT is in your wallet, moving it again costs **BNB** for gas on BSC. If you withdraw only USDT and zero BNB, you can be stuck looking at a balance you cannot move. You will buy a little BNB on purpose. That BNB is part of the first-buy cost, even if you did not think of it as a “fee.”

TABLE
Line | When it hits | How to see it
P2P / on-ramp spread | When local money becomes a book-entry | Compare several adverts or corridor quotes; do not worship one screenshot
Bank or card charge | When fiat leaves your account | Bank SMS, card statement, FX markup
Trading fee | When you click buy or sell | Fee schedule + order receipt
Spread | During the trade | Bid versus ask
Withdrawal fee | When you leave | Withdrawal screen, before you confirm
Gas | On-chain moves later | Wallet estimate; needs BNB on BSC
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Alex “buys 100 USDT.”

1. He pays 164,000 local currency to a P2P seller whose advert was a higher quote. A blog said 1,610. The 30 local currency per unit is the on-ramp spread.
2. He then market-buys a tiny alt, pays a 0.1% taker fee, and pays a wide spread on a thin book.
3. He withdraws USDT on ERC-20 “because the letters look serious.”
4. The withdrawal fee plus Ethereum gas eats a painful chunk of a 100 USDT stack.
5. He writes “crypto is a scam.” Several of those lines were **choices**, not physics. The chain did not pick ERC-20 for him.

DIAGRAM
Local money
   -> P2P / bank / card spread
   -> CEX book-entry
   -> trading fee + spread
   -> withdrawal fee
   -> on-chain gas (BNB on BSC)
   = what you still control
ENDDIAGRAM

## How to read a withdrawal screen

Before you confirm a withdraw, the screen must answer:

- **Asset** (USDT is not BNB)
- **Network** (BEP-20 / BSC is not ERC-20 is not TRC-20)
- **Destination address** (yours, copied from your wallet on that network)
- **Amount you send** versus **amount they receive**
- **Fee**

If any line is fuzzy, do not confirm. A 1 USDT or smallest-allowed **test send** exists for this reason. Module 5 is the ritual.

Cheap plus wrong network is not cheap. Paying a slightly higher withdrawal fee on the **correct** network is cheaper than a perfect fee on the wrong one.

## What “zero fee” usually hides

Promotions that say “zero trading fees” often keep spread, withdrawal fees, and P2P markup. A pair with “zero maker fees” can still hurt a taker. Read the receipt, not the banner.

Card buys inside an app are famous for this: a comfortable button, a painful all-in FX rate. If you cannot see the all-in price before you confirm, you are not shopping. You are being billed.

NOTE
Nobody in this academy is graded on getting the absolute cheapest fee. You are graded on not vanishing the stack. A slightly worse rate inside a platform with escrow is often cheaper than a “best rate” on WhatsApp with no parent. Academy paid-track checkout, when live, is USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout — a published rail, not a discounted chat wallet.
ENDNOTE

## Write the all-in on paper once

Before you call a fill “fine,” write four numbers:

1. Local currency that left your bank (or card).
2. USDT IOU that appeared (or crypto IOU).
3. Trading fee plus estimated spread on any conversion.
4. Planned withdrawal fee plus a little BNB for later gas.

Divide (1) by what you will still control after (4). That is your real rate. If you cannot write the four numbers, you are not ready to compare this CEX to a WhatsApp desk. The desk will always quote one pretty number and hide the rest.

VIP fee tiers, referral codes, and “zero maker” months are optional later. First-buy literacy is the four lines. A cheaper taker fee on the wrong network is still the expensive choice.

## What this lesson is for

You should be able to reconstruct the all-in price of a first buy on paper, including the BNB you will need later, without calling the missing USDT “theft.”

## Say this out loud

- Chart price is not the bill. The bill is spread plus fees plus later gas.
- Withdrawal fee and gas are part of the first-buy cost.
- On BSC you will need BNB to move tokens later. That BNB is not optional decoration.
- Cheap plus wrong network is not cheap.
- “Zero fee” usually moved the cost to another line.

Next: the last distinction in this module — an IOU you cannot spend on-chain versus coins you can withdraw.

lessons.title: Custodial IOUs versus coins you can withdraw
lessons.content:
# Custodial IOUs versus coins you can withdraw

The most expensive confusion in beginner crypto is this: the number on an exchange screen is treated as coins in a wallet. It is not. It is a **custodial IOU**.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to point at a balance and say whether you are a customer of a company or a key-holder on a chain, what “withdraw” actually does, and why “I bought, so it is in my wallet already” is false. **Custody** means: who holds the keys that can sign a spend.

## Custodial means they hold the keys

When you buy USDT on a CEX, the company (or their custodian bank of wallets) holds the private keys to large addresses. Your 50 USDT is a row: “this customer is owed 50.” Thousands of customers can be owed USDT that sits, pooled, in a handful of on-chain addresses the company controls.

That design is how exchanges stay fast. Internal trades do not hit the chain. They rewrite rows. That is also why BscScan does not show your email.

**Non-custodial** (self-custody) means: keys you control can sign. The wallets course trained that habit. This course does not replace it. Moving from IOU to wallet is Module 6, and only after those habits.

## What you can do with an IOU

With an exchange balance you can typically:

- trade it for another IOU on that platform (spot)
- sometimes send it to another user of the **same** platform (internal transfer — still their ledger)
- request a **withdrawal** to an address on a chain

You cannot:

- paste the exchange screen into BscScan and find “your” coins
- sign a DEX swap with that balance
- pay on-chain gas from a CEX USDT row without withdrawing
- prove to a stranger that you “hold” a token on-chain

Internal transfers feel like blockchain sends. They are chat between two rows. No public hash. If the company reverses them, the chain was never involved.

TABLE
State | Where the coins live | What you hold | Who can freeze it
Funded, not withdrawn | Company wallets, pooled | An IOU | The company, courts, their risk team
Withdrawn, confirmed | The chain you chose | Coins at your address | Nobody’s help desk; the keys decide
Stuck on a withdrawal | In flight, or already on a chain | A ticket plus an explorer lookup | Mix of company process and chain finality
Wrong-network send | A chain you were not watching | Maybe recoverable, often painful | Panic does not help
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Fatima buys 80 USDT and 0.03 BNB on an example CEX. She screenshots the balances and posts “I’m on-chain now.”

1. She is not. Both numbers are IOUs.
2. She starts a USDT withdrawal on BEP-20 to her Trust Wallet — an example of a wallet app, not an endorsement — address on BNB Smart Chain.
3. After confirmations, BscScan shows a token transfer to her address. Now that slice is on-chain.
4. The BNB still on the exchange is still an IOU. Two books, two truths.
5. If she then tells a group “the exchange and BscScan disagree,” they should. She has not withdrawn the BNB yet.

DIAGRAM
[ CEX database ]
  Fatima: 80 USDT IOU
  Fatima: 0.03 BNB IOU
        |
        |  withdraw USDT BEP-20
        v
[ BNB Smart Chain ]
  Fatima's 0x address: 80 USDT (BEP-20)
  Fatima's 0x address: 0 BNB   (until she also withdraws BNB)

Two screens. They SHOULD disagree until both withdrawals land.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Withdrawal is a company sending from their keys to yours

A withdrawal is not “download my coins.” It is:

1. You ask the company to reduce your IOU.
2. Their risk engine checks KYC, limits, whitelist, travel-rule data, fraud flags.
3. If yes, they sign an on-chain transaction from **their** address to **yours**.
4. The chain includes it. Explorers show it.
5. Their database marks your row down.

If step 2 says no, nothing hit the chain. You still have (or had) an IOU and a ticket. “The blockchain is slow” is the wrong sentence. The company has not broadcast yet.

## Insolvency, halts, and why size still matters

If a company cannot honour withdrawals, customers become creditors. That has happened to platforms with huge brands. This academy is not predicting any named firm will fail. It is telling you the legal shape: an IOU is a claim, not a UTXO.

Practice size is how adults sleep. You do not need to withdraw every unit the hour you buy. You do need to know that un-withdrawn size is company risk plus login risk.

NOTE
“I bought so it is in my wallet already” is the misconception this module exists to kill. A wallet you control is an address whose keys you hold. An exchange spot buy is a row. Academy checkout, when live, is USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout to a published flow — still not “your exchange screenshot is payment.”
ENDNOTE

## Why internal books exist, without romance

Matching trades on-chain for every tiny fill would be slow and expensive. Companies keep an internal book so that 10,000 customers can buy and sell USDT with each other without 10,000 BscScan rows. That convenience is the product. The cost is that you are waiting on their solvency, their support hours, and their risk engine.

You may keep practice size as IOU while you finish Wallets habits. You may withdraw when the destination is ready. Both are allowed. What is not allowed is pointing at the IOU and telling a group you are “on BSC now.” Words are part of safety. Wrong words recruit helpers.

## What this lesson is for

You should now be able to hear “I have USDT” and ask the only adult follow-up: **where?** Company book, or which chain?

## Say this out loud

- A custodial balance is an IOU. Coins you can spend on-chain start after a withdrawal confirms.
- Internal transfers on an exchange are still their ledger.
- Withdrawal is the company signing from their keys to yours, after their risk engine says yes.
- Exchange screen and explorer should disagree until you withdraw.
- This is still not a buy order for Crystal Stones or any other ticker.

Next module: the account itself — arriving at the real site, KYC, 2FA, and the humans who will try to talk the door open.

lessons.title: Arriving at the real site (bookmarks, ads, clones)
lessons.content:
# Arriving at the real site (bookmarks, ads, clones)

The most expensive click in this course is not “Buy.” It is **Login** on a fake domain.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to describe how you will open an exchange for the rest of your life, why ads and chat links are hostile until proven, and what to do if you already typed a password into a maybe-fake page. **Phishing** means: a fake page or app that looks like the real company, built to capture your login, your 2FA code, or both, in real time.

## The bookmark ritual

Do this on a calm day, from a device you trust, before you have money on the account.

1. Type the brand into a search engine **once**, or better, use a URL you verified from more than one independent source — the company’s official X account, a long-standing app-store listing, documentation you already trust. Do not treat the first sponsored result as the company.
2. Check the domain character by character. `binance.com` is not `binance.com.security-login.ru`. A hyphen, an extra word, a unicode lookalike, a `.net` instead of `.com` — all of these have emptied accounts. Binance is an example of a centralised exchange here, not a command to use it.
3. Bookmark it.
4. Forever after, open the bookmark. Do not use the ad. Do not use the SMS. Do not use the pinned Telegram “login helper.”

The ritual feels fussy until the day you are panicked. Panic is when clones convert.

TABLE
Arrival method | Verdict
Bookmark you saved on a calm day | Default
Official app from the real Apple / Google store listing you verified | Acceptable; still check the publisher name
Sponsored search ad | Hostile until proven
Link in email “withdrawals paused, login” | Hostile
Link in WhatsApp from “support” | Hostile
QR code on a flyer at a meetup you did not organise | Hostile until you type the domain yourself
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student searches “Binance login,” taps the first ad, lands on a page that looks perfect, types email, password, and the authenticator code.

1. The phish relays the code in real time to the real site.
2. The student is logged in on the attacker’s session.
3. The withdrawal whitelist is empty. The stack is gone in minutes.
4. The real platform later says: we see a login from another device.
5. The chain did nothing. The door was the ad. BscScan has no row called “stolen by Google Ads.”

DIAGRAM
Calm day: verify domain --> bookmark --> only that
Panic day: email / SMS / ad --> clone --> they have the session

The clone does not need your seed.
It needs the login plus the 2FA you type while scared.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Apps versus browsers

A phone app from the official store reduces some phishing (you do not type a URL). It does not remove:

- fake apps with similar names
- overlay malware that draws a fake login on top of the real app
- a support chat inside a cloned APK
- a “helper” who wants remote desktop “to install it for you”

Install count and publisher name matter. Side-loading an APK “because the group dropped it” is how wallet clones harvest seeds — and how exchange clones harvest logins. An exchange login is not a seed. Both are still secrets. Academy staff will never ask for either.

If you use a browser on a shared cybercafe computer, assume the password is burned when you stand up. Public machines are not a security model.

## Homograph and subdomain tricks

Look carefully at:

- `xn--` domains (punycode) that render as familiar letters
- `login-brand.something-else.com` — the real brand is not the registrable domain
- extra words: `brand-wallet.com`, `brandweb3.net`
- URL shorteners in SMS

Read the address bar, not the logo. Logos are copy-paste.

## If you already typed it

If you already typed a password into a maybe-fake page, treat it as burned.

- From a **different** device if you can, open the **bookmarked** real site
- Change the password
- Enable or rotate 2FA
- Check sessions and devices
- Check withdrawal whitelist
- Move funds if the account still exists and you still control it

Do not “see if they logged in.” Assume they did. Speed beats dignity.

NOTE
Crystal Stones Academy will never send you a “login to keep your progress” link that is not the site you already bookmarked. We will never ask for an exchange password. If a message uses our name and wants a login, it is a clone of us, not us.
ENDNOTE

## Shared phones, family, and “just login for me”

A second beginner hole: someone you trust wants to “show you how.” They take the phone, type the password, maybe screenshot 2FA “so it is easier next time.” You have just expanded the session to a person who can be phished later, or who can panic-send.

If you must learn with a relative in the room, they watch. They do not type. They do not photograph. They do not keep the SIM. A family member with your SMS 2FA is a SIM-swap with extra steps.

Also refuse “let me send you the login link I use.” Their bookmark is not yours. Their SMS is not yours. Build your own calm-day door.

Public Wi-Fi plus a browser exchange login is how cafe sessions linger. Prefer the official app after you verified the publisher, or wait until you are on a network you trust. Convenience is how clones convert on travel days.

## What this lesson is for

You should have one boring door into any CEX you use, and a reflex that ads, emails, and chat buttons are not that door.

## Say this out loud

- Bookmark the real domain on a calm day. That is how you arrive forever after.
- Ads, emails, and chat links are hostile until proven.
- A clone can relay 2FA in real time and steal the session without a seed.
- Fake apps exist in stores and especially outside them.
- If you typed a password on a maybe-fake page, treat it as burned and rotate from the bookmark.

Next: KYC — what you are actually handing over, and why this academy will not tell you to fake it.

lessons.title: KYC without folklore (what it is for, what it is not)
lessons.content:
# KYC without folklore (what it is for, what it is not)

**KYC** means Know Your Customer. The company records identity because regulators, banks, and their own risk team demand it.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what KYC is for from the company’s side, what it does **not** guarantee for you, and why bought accounts and “helpers” who upload your ID are how people lose both money and a legal story. You will usually send a government ID, a selfie or liveness check, sometimes proof of address, and sometimes questions about source of funds if amounts grow.

## What KYC is for (from the company’s side)

- they want bank rails and licenses
- they want to refuse sanctioned names
- they want to show an auditor they tried
- they want a freeze handle if law enforcement asks
- they want to make card and bank partners less nervous

None of that is folklore. It is the price of connecting a crypto company to the banking system. You can dislike it. You still need to understand it.

In Nigeria this often collides with BVN, NIN, and bank-name matching. In other countries it collides with passports, tax IDs, and proof of address. The paperwork changes. The idea does not: the company wants a human they can name.

## What KYC is not

- It is not a guarantee the company is honest
- It is not a guarantee your coins are safe
- It is not the same as self-custody
- It is not optional on many major CEX on-ramps, even if a Telegram thread says “KYC is slavery”
- It is not Crystal Stones Academy collecting your passport in a mentor chat

A licensed firm can still be hacked, slow, or rude. An unlicensed desk can still steal. KYC is identity, not insurance.

Using stolen IDs, bought “verification services,” or someone else’s BVN is **fraud**. This academy will not help you do that. If a platform is not available in your country, that is a jurisdiction fact, not a puzzle to cheat.

TABLE
Honest path | Dishonest path this course will not teach
Use a platform that serves your country, with your own documents | Bought KYC, VPN theatre to evade residency rules, cousin’s ID
Stay small on P2P with your own bank account, understanding the risk | Money-mule accounts, “receive for me”
If you cannot use a major CEX, use a licensed local on-ramp or wait | Fake papers
Minimise how many platforms hold your ID | Post your ID selfie in a group “for help”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A group sells “KYC done accounts.” The buyer gets an exchange login.

1. Months later the original identity files a complaint, or the real owner recovers email.
2. The account is frozen with the buyer’s USDT inside.
3. The buyer has no legal story that does not start with “I bought a stolen identity.”
4. Support will not side with the person who is not the name on the file.
5. Do not do this. There is no academy workaround.

DIAGRAM
You  -->  exchange compliance (expected, under their terms)
You  -->  random helper in chat (how accounts get stolen)

Academy login email  is not  an exchange KYC pack
We still will not ask for your seed, your BVN, or your ID card in a mentor chat.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Privacy versus secrecy

You can still:

- minimise how many platforms hold your ID
- not post your ID selfie in a group
- not send KYC photos through WhatsApp “helpers” who offer to upload for you
- use a platform that actually serves your country rather than collecting five grey-market logins

A helper who wants your ID photos plus selfie plus SMS codes is not helping. They are taking the account. **Secrecy** would mean hiding from the law. This academy will not teach that. **Privacy** means not broadcasting your documents to strangers who do not need them.

Source-of-funds questions at larger sizes are also not a personal insult. They are the company protecting their banking relationships. Answer honestly or do not use that corridor. Lying on those forms is another kind of fraud.

## When KYC meets withdrawals

A completed KYC file is often what lets larger withdrawals through. It can also be what lets a freeze land on a named human. Both are true. If you want bank rails, you are visible to that company. If you want to be only a key on a chain, you withdraw — after the Wallets course habits — and you accept that the on-ramp still saw you.

NOTE
Crystal Stones Academy collecting an email for login is not the same as an exchange KYC pack. We still will not ask for your seed, your BVN, or your ID card in a mentor chat. Paid-track checkout, when live, is USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout, not a request for your passport in WhatsApp.
ENDNOTE

## What happens to the pictures

Your ID images sit on the company’s servers, and often on a vendor that does liveness checks. That is a data-hold. It is not a reason to use a fake. It is a reason not to multiply copies: no WhatsApp helpers, no “KYC agent” Telegram, no posting a selfie-with-passport in a group to prove you are real.

If a platform is blocked in your country, the adult options are: use a platform that serves you, use a smaller local on-ramp that is actually allowed, or wait. VPN-plus-foreign-ID is how accounts get closed with the IOU inside. This academy will not map that maze.

Source-of-wealth questions at larger sizes can feel nosy. They are the banking system talking through the CEX. Answer or do not use that size. Do not invent a story about “consultancy” if the local currency was a salary. Lies on those forms follow the KYC name — yours.

## What this lesson is for

You should be able to complete or refuse KYC as an adult: your documents, their terms, no folklore, no rented identity.

## Say this out loud

- KYC is identity for a company that holds an IOU. It does not make the IOU on-chain.
- KYC is not a honesty stamp and not insurance.
- Fake KYC is fraud, not a life hack.
- Nobody should upload your ID “for you” in chat.
- Privacy is not posting documents. Secrecy from the law is not this course.

Next: 2FA that actually changes the outcome.

lessons.title: 2FA that actually works (authenticator vs SMS)
lessons.content:
# 2FA that actually works (authenticator vs SMS)

**Two-factor authentication** means: password is not enough. The second factor is something the thief should not also have.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to rank SMS, authenticator apps, and hardware keys, say why “SMS 2FA is enough” is a dangerous sentence, and describe how you will back up an authenticator secret without photographing it into WhatsApp. An exchange login is not a seed. 2FA is still a door into the company that holds your IOU.

## SMS is better than nothing and worse than people think

A code sent to your phone number. Problems:

- **SIM swap**: someone convinces the mobile operator they are you, takes the number, receives the SMS
- SMS can be read by malware or by a cloned notification
- operators and “customer care” are social-engineering targets
- SS7 and related telecom attacks exist; you do not need the engineering, you need the conclusion

Use SMS if the platform offers nothing else. Do not stay there. In Nigeria, SIM-registration stories and “customer care” theatre make this more than a Western blog scare. In other countries the same attack has a different script: port-out fraud, prepaid swap, a call to the carrier with last-four of an ID.

SMS 2FA is not “enough.” It is a step above a password alone.

## Authenticator apps (TOTP)

**TOTP** means time-based one-time password: Google Authenticator, Authy, Aegis, and similar generate a rotating code from a **secret** that was shown as a QR when you enabled 2FA. Trust Wallet and MetaMask are examples of wallet apps, not 2FA apps — do not confuse them. An authenticator is a code clock. A wallet holds keys.

Rules:

- screenshotting the QR into WhatsApp is how 2FA gets stolen
- if you lose the phone **and** have no backup of the 2FA secret, you are in a support queue to recover the exchange
- write the 2FA backup codes / seed **on paper**, store with the same seriousness as a wallet seed — it is not a chain seed, but it opens the company door
- cloud-backed authenticators are convenient and are another account to harden

The 2FA secret is not your wallet seed. Do not store them on the same photo roll titled “crypto.” If that roll leaks, the thief has the exchange and a map to the wallet.

## Hardware keys (FIDO / passkeys)

YubiKey and similar. You tap a physical device. Phishing sites have a harder time relaying this, because the key checks the real domain. If the exchange supports it for login **and** for withdrawals, this is the adult setting. Module 2’s last lesson returns to passkeys and sessions.

TABLE
Method | Protects against casual password leak? | Fails when
SMS | Somewhat | SIM swap, operator social engineering
Authenticator app | Yes, if the secret is not photographed into the cloud | Phone loss without backup; malware reading the screen; real-time phish if you type the code into a clone
Hardware key | Best of the common options | You lose the keys and the backup; you approve a prompt you did not understand
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student’s exchange password leaks in an old data breach.

1. Attacker tries login. SMS 2FA is on, but the student’s mobile number is on a SIM registered with a weak “security question.”
2. SIM swap on a Friday. Weekend withdrawals empty the account.
3. Authenticator on a separate device, plus a **withdrawal whitelist** (next lesson), would have changed the story.
4. The chain did not fail. Telecom and a weak second factor failed.
5. “I had 2FA” is not a complete sentence. Which 2FA?

DIAGRAM
Password  --+
            +-->  both required  -->  session
2FA       --+

If the 2FA lives on the same stolen phone as the email,
you built one door with two locks on the same hinge.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Separate the doors

Ideally:

- email password ≠ exchange password ≠ wallet PIN
- 2FA for email is not SMS on the same SIM as exchange SMS
- recovery codes on paper, not in the same Google account that receives the exchange email
- the phone that receives email is not the only copy of the authenticator

This is annoying. It is cheaper than an emptied account.

Disable 2FA only when the platform forces a reset, and only on the bookmarked site. A popup saying “2FA expired, turn off to continue” is a classic steal.

NOTE
Academy staff will never ask you to read a 2FA code into a chat, a voice call, or a remote-desktop session. Real support does not need the code. A thief does. SMS 2FA is not enough; do not type any 2FA into a page you arrived at from panic.
ENDNOTE

## Losing the phone without losing the account

Plan the ugly day. Phone in a motorcycle taxi. Authenticator gone.

If you wrote the TOTP backup codes on paper, you restore the authenticator on a new device and keep the exchange. If the only copy was the old phone and SMS is the fallback on the same SIM you also lost, you are in a support queue with KYC selfies. That queue is slow. It is still better than a thief with SMS.

So: paper backup of 2FA in a place that is not the phone. Second device if you can afford it. Email 2FA not on the same SIM. This is housekeeping, not paranoia. People skip it because the QR was annoying on day one. Day one is when you still have time.

A password manager can store TOTP if you already trust that manager with a strong master password and its own 2FA. Do not invent a new cloud just for this. Do not put TOTP in the same camera roll as a wallet seed.

## What this lesson is for

You should leave SMS as a stopgap, turn on an authenticator with a paper backup, and stop saying “I have 2FA” as if all second factors were equal.

## Say this out loud

- SMS 2FA loses to SIM swap. It is not enough.
- Authenticator is the minimum grown-up setting. Backup the secret on paper.
- Do not type 2FA into a page you arrived at from panic. Clones relay codes in real time.
- Do not store the 2FA QR next to a wallet seed in the same camera roll.
- Hardware keys beat typed codes when the platform offers them.

Next: withdrawal whitelist, anti-phishing codes, and device lists.

lessons.title: Withdrawal whitelist, anti-phishing codes, device list
lessons.content:
# Withdrawal whitelist, anti-phishing codes, device list

Login theft is not the end of the story unless withdrawals are easy. You want withdrawals to be **sticky**.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to turn on three controls that turn a stolen session into a race you can still win: an address whitelist, an anti-phishing code, and a habit of reading the device list. A **withdrawal whitelist** means: the company will only send coins to addresses you already approved, often after a delay when you add a new one.

## Withdrawal address whitelist

Many CEX let you lock withdrawals to **known addresses** you control. Adding a new address emails you and waits (often 24 hours). A thief who has today’s session still cannot send to their address until that delay passes — time for you to see the email and freeze.

Practical academy setup:

1. Create your self-custody address on BNB Smart Chain (you did this conceptually in the wallets course).
2. After a **tiny** test, whitelist **that** address for USDT and for BNB.
3. Leave whitelist **on**. The inconvenience is the feature.

If you need a new address, you wait. That wait is cheaper than a drain. Never whitelist an address a “broker,” “mentor,” or “academy agent” pasted. If someone wants to be paid, they can wait for a test send you initiated to an address **you** verified. Intermediate tuition is not collected by a new wallet in a DM. When paid tracks go live, checkout is USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout — a published flow, not a whitelist entry from chat.

## Anti-phishing codes

An **anti-phishing code** is a word **you** choose that the real exchange embeds in its emails. If an email looks like Binance — an example of a centralised exchange — but does not show your code, it is fake. Set a code that is not your dog’s name posted on Instagram, not “CrystalStones,” not “1234.”

The code does not encrypt anything. It is a glance test. Use it. Read emails for it before you click anything. Prefer still to open the bookmark rather than the button.

## Device and session lists

Open the security page on a calm day. Learn what “this device” looks like. If you see a city you were not in, kick the session, rotate password and 2FA, check whitelist.

New device emails are not noise. They are the alarm. If you just logged in from a new phone, you should recognise the mail. If you did not, act as if the session is hostile.

## Withdrawal lock / cooling-off

Some platforms pause withdrawals after a password change or a new device. Do not disable every safety timer because it slowed you down once. Thieves hate timers. That is the point.

Some platforms also let you set a **withdrawal password** separate from login. If offered, use a different secret. One password for everything is one leak for everything.

TABLE
Control | What it buys you | How people turn it off
Address whitelist | Thief cannot instantly reroute | “I’ll just disable for this one send”
Anti-phishing word | Fake emails fail a glance test | Never set it
Device list | You notice a stranger session | Never look
Email for withdrawal | A second channel of alarm | Using an email they already have 2FA-less
Cooling-off after password change | Time | “Too annoying, I trade daily”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Attacker has password plus 2FA from a cloned login page. They request a withdrawal to a new address.

1. Whitelist is on; the new address is not listed.
2. The platform refuses or starts a 24h wait and emails the student.
3. The student, who actually reads security mail on a bookmarked app, kills sessions, rotates 2FA, keeps the whitelist on.
4. Without whitelist, the story ends at “withdrawal complete.”
5. The coins never needed a seed. They needed a sticky withdrawal door.

DIAGRAM
Stolen session
    |
    v
Can they withdraw to a new address?
    |
    +-- whitelist ON, delay ON --> you have time
    +-- whitelist OFF --> stack is gone
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Whitelist the address **you** created, not an address a “broker” or “academy agent” pasted. Academy staff will never ask you to whitelist a Crystal Stones treasury, a the checkout processor address from chat, or a PaynovaX wallet. Published checkout, when it exists, is not a DM.
ENDNOTE

## Adding the first address without bypassing the delay

The 24-hour wait when you add an address feels like the company is insulting you. It is the feature that makes a stolen session survive until morning. Do not file a ticket to “please speed whitelist, I am a VIP.” Thieves file that ticket too.

Add **your** BSC address after a tiny on-chain test has already landed, so you know the string is right. If you whitelist a mistyped address, you have built a sticky door to a void. Test, then whitelist, then leave it on.

If you must withdraw to a new address — new wallet after a phone death — accept the delay. Park the IOU. Anyone offering an “instant whitelist bypass” is offering to steal the delay from you.

## Glance tests only work if you glance

Keep the anti-phishing word somewhere you will actually look on mail days. Instant whitelist bypasses are theft of the delay. Test the address on-chain first so you do not whitelist a mistype to a void.

## What this lesson is for

You should treat whitelist, anti-phishing codes, and device lists as part of opening the account — not as extras for “serious traders.”

## Say this out loud

- Whitelist turns a stolen session into a race you can still win.
- Anti-phishing codes make fake mail look fake. Still open the bookmark, not the button.
- Safety delays are not the enemy.
- Never whitelist a stranger’s address, including one that claims to be this academy.
- Check the device list on a calm day so a strange city is obvious.

Next: fake support, fake emails, fake job offers — the human interface to all of the above.

lessons.title: Fake support, fake emails, fake job offers
lessons.content:
# Fake support, fake emails, fake job offers

Once you have an exchange account, you become a target for people who will **talk** you into opening the door.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name the three common human scripts — fake support, fake security email, fake job — and refuse them without a debate. **Social engineering** means: they do not break the cryptography. They break you.

## The support impersonator

You tweet or post in a Telegram group that a withdrawal is stuck. Within minutes, “Binance Support” or “Crystal Stones Admin” DMs you. They have a badge they awarded themselves. They want:

- a screen share
- a “verification code”
- a seed (for a wallet problem that they have mapped onto your CEX panic)
- a login on a “ticket portal”

Real support sits behind the **bookmarked app**. They do not cold-DM you first. Crystal Stones Academy mentor chat will not ask for seeds, 2FA codes, or screen-control of your exchange. Support will not withdraw for you. Anyone who offers to “process the withdrawal from our side” is not support.

## The security email

“Unusual login, click here.” You already know: bookmark, not the button. Check the anti-phishing word. If it is missing, it is fake. If it is present, still open the bookmark — codes can be stolen from layouts, and HTML is cheap.

SMS versions exist: “Your account will be closed in 30 minutes.” The timer is the hook. Real risk teams do not need you to sprint through a shortened URL.

## The job / task offer

“Earn 2% per day executing trades for our desk. We deposit USDT, you forward it.” You are being recruited as a **mule**. The coins are stolen. When they bounce, your KYC is on the account that moved them. Decline.

Variants: “liquidity provider onboarding,” “test our new P2P desk,” “you are selected as a regional agent for Crystal Stones.” This academy does not hire through DMs to move coins. We do not pay salaries in forwarded USDT.

## The recovery helper

“Your 2FA is broken, send the QR, I will reset.” No.

“Send 50 USDT to this verification wallet to unlock withdrawals.” No. That is a second invoice, not a fix.

TABLE
Ask | Real support | Thief
Seed phrase | Never | Always eventually
2FA code in chat | Never | “to verify it is you”
Remote desktop | Never | “so I can see the error”
Deposit to a new address to “unlock” | Never | Standard
Work inside the bookmarked app ticket | Yes | They hate this
Withdraw on your behalf | No — you click withdraw | “We will process it”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student’s withdrawal is delayed for compliance — a real, boring delay.

1. A helpful admin on WhatsApp says send 50 USDT to a “verification wallet” to prove ownership.
2. The student pays. The delay was going to clear anyway. The 50 USDT is extra theft.
3. Always separate **the company’s slow process** from **a stranger’s urgent invoice**.
4. The student opens a ticket in the bookmarked app and waits.
5. No seed was requested this time. The money still left because the script sounded official.

DIAGRAM
Problem happens
    |
    +--> official app ticket --> wait, boring, sometimes works
    +--> DM that arrived after you posted --> assume thief
ENDDIAGRAM

## What real delays look like

Compliance holds, travel-rule questionnaires, weekend queues, and “we need a selfie again” are dull. They happen inside the app. They do not require you to pay a release fee to a new address. If the official ticket says wait, you wait. If a DM says pay, you do not.

Travel-rule extra questions — “who is the beneficiary, what is this for” — can appear on larger withdrawals. That is a company-and-law process. It is not a stranger in Telegram collecting a screenshot of your seed. Answer inside the ticket. Do not answer in a parallel chat that arrived second.

Phone calls exist too. A voice that says they are compliance and asks you to read a 2FA code is a thief with a phone. Real firms almost never need you to read a rotating code aloud. Hang up. Open the bookmark. See if a ticket you already opened asked for a call back on a number published in their help centre — not a number the caller dictated.

## Crystal Stones clothing on the same scripts

Because you are in this academy, you will also meet clones of **us**. They will offer “priority listing,” “mentor allocation,” or “the checkout processor is down, use this wallet.” USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout is the published checkout when paid tracks go live. It is not a Telegram wallet. It is not PaynovaX. It is not Crystal Stone token. Staff will not withdraw for you, will not take a seed, and will not send a job that is “forward this USDT.”

NOTE
If you are actually stuck, log in from the bookmark, open support, and wait. Use a second channel only if **you** initiated it from documentation you already trusted. Do not let the thief pick the channel. Support will not withdraw for you. Academy staff will not either.
ENDNOTE

## Why they know your ticket number

Some scams scrape public tweets or group screenshots that include a ticket ID, then DM “we saw case 483920.” A number is not proof they are the company. The company already has the case inside the app.

Similarly, job offers that know your KYC name from a leaked database will feel personal. Personal is not official. Official is the bookmark.

If you already sent a 2FA code to a DM, treat the account as compromised this hour: other device, bookmark, kill sessions, freeze, rotate. Shame is slower than a withdrawal. Do the freeze first. Tell the real ticket later that a clone harvested a code. Do not tell the clone you are onto them while they still have a session.

## What this lesson is for

You should treat unsolicited help as an attack until the ticket you opened inside the real app says otherwise.

## Say this out loud

- Support does not first-DM you. Support will not withdraw for you.
- Nobody needs your 2FA code, seed, or screen share in chat.
- “Earn by forwarding USDT” is mule work. Your KYC becomes the exit node.
- Official and slow beats unofficial and urgent.
- A verification wallet to “unlock” withdrawals is a second theft.

Next: passkeys, sessions, and when to freeze the account.

lessons.title: Passkeys, sessions, and when to freeze the account
lessons.content:
# Passkeys, sessions, and when to freeze the account

Passwords leak. Sessions linger. Adults need a freeze reflex.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what a **session** is, what a **passkey** is, when to kill every session, and when to freeze withdrawals rather than “wait and see.” This is still login security, not a seed. An exchange freeze is a company button. A wallet freeze does not exist — that is the wallets course.

## What a session is

When you log in, the company hands your browser or app a **session token**: a secret cookie or app credential that says “this device is already you.” That is why you are not typing a password every tap. It is also why a stolen session can spend without re-typing the password until it expires or you kick it.

Sessions live until:

- you log out
- you kill them on the device-list page
- they expire
- the company invalidates them after a password change (if they bother)

“I closed the tab” is not logout. “I deleted the app” is not always logout. Open the security page and look.

## Passkeys, in plain language

A **passkey** is a login secret stored in your device’s secure hardware (or a password manager that supports the standard), unlocking with your face, fingerprint, or device PIN. The site never sees a password you can type into a clone. The passkey is bound to the real domain more tightly than a password.

If your CEX offers passkeys or security keys for login, turn them on in addition to, not instead of, a still-protected email. Keep a backup method you control. Losing the only phone with the only passkey is a support queue.

Passkeys are not seeds. They open the company. They do not move on-chain coins by themselves.

## When to freeze

Freeze (disable withdrawals, lock the account, kick sessions) when:

- you typed a password or 2FA on a maybe-fake page
- you see a device or city you were not in
- you received a withdrawal email you did not start
- your email was reset without you
- a “support” person had remote desktop, even “briefly”
- your SIM stopped working and you did not request a replacement

Do not wait to “see if anything happens.” Assume the session is already spending.

Practical order:

1. From a different device, bookmark, login (or account-recovery through official support).
2. Kill all sessions.
3. Change password. Rotate 2FA.
4. Confirm whitelist is on and only your addresses.
5. Freeze withdrawals if the platform has that button.
6. Only then look at balances.

TABLE
Signal | Action
Unknown device on the list | Kick all sessions, rotate secrets, freeze withdrawals
Withdrawal email you did not start | Freeze first, argue later
SIM dead without you | Treat exchange SMS 2FA as burned; freeze from another channel
Remote desktop with “support” | Freeze. The account is compromised. Dignity later.
Passkey prompt you did not start | Deny. Then sessions page.
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Ijeoma’s phone shows a passkey prompt for her example CEX while she is cooking. She did not open the app.

1. She denies the prompt.
2. She does not tap “yes” to make the popup go away.
3. From a laptop she already bookmarked, she opens the real site, kills sessions, freezes withdrawals.
4. She finds a login attempt from another country.
5. Because whitelist was on, nothing left. The freeze was still correct. “Nothing left” is not a reason to skip the freeze next time.

DIAGRAM
Odd signal (prompt, email, dead SIM, strange city)
        |
        v
Deny / ignore the stranger's channel
        |
        v
Bookmark on a second device --> kill sessions --> freeze withdrawals
        |
        v
Rotate password + 2FA --> read whitelist --> then look at balances
ENDDIAGRAM

## Email is part of the account

If the thief has the email, password-reset is their tool. Put 2FA on email. Prefer authenticator or passkeys there too. An exchange with perfect 2FA and an email on SMS-only is a chain with a weak link labelled “forgot password.”

NOTE
Freezing is reversible through official support. Sending coins to a “safe holding address” a stranger just pasted is often the actual theft. Freeze the company account. Do not “rescue” funds to a new wallet you have not verified with Wallets-course habits, and never to an address from chat.
ENDNOTE

## Shared computers and leftover sessions

Internet-cafe or library logins leave sessions on machines you will never see again. If you ever used one, assume it is still live until you kill **all** sessions from a machine you own. Log out is a button. Session list is the proof.

Passkeys on a shared family tablet can let a relative approve a prompt they do not understand. If the device is communal, do not store the only passkey there. Prefer a device that is yours, plus a backup method you control.

Freeze is not a moral failure. It is a switch. Unfreezing through official support is allowed. Sending leftover IOUs to a “holding wallet” a voice on the phone just dictated is how freezes get converted into theft.

## What this lesson is for

You should have a freeze checklist you can run while scared, without asking a group what to do.

## Say this out loud

- A session is a lingering “already logged in.” Closing a tab is not logout.
- Passkeys bind login to the real domain better than typed passwords. They are not seeds.
- Odd prompt, odd email, dead SIM: freeze first, balances later.
- Kill all sessions, rotate secrets, confirm whitelist.
- Do not rescue funds to an address a stranger pasted.

Take the quiz. Then we fund the account — how local money becomes a book-entry without becoming a P2P casualty.
