lessons.title: How local money becomes a book-entry
lessons.content:
# How local money becomes a book-entry

You cannot wire local currency to BNB Smart Chain. You cannot wire dollars into a BEP-20 contract either. A human process sits in the middle. Local money becomes a **book-entry**: a row on a company’s ledger that says they owe you crypto, or — if you used a broker — a hope that someone else sent coins.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name the three common doors (platform deposit, in-app P2P, off-platform human), say which one has a parent, and refuse the sentence “I paid, so I am on-chain.” **On-ramp** means: the process that turns national currency into an exchange IOU or into coins. It is not a chain feature.

## 1. Platform deposit from a bank or card

Some exchanges and local on-ramps let you send local currency from **your** bank name to **their** corporate account, or pay a card. In other countries the corridor might be a bank transfer, SEPA, ACH, Faster Payments, or a card processor. The name on the sending account should match KYC. Paying from a friend’s account is how compliance freezes start.

Delays are real. Weekend banking is real. A receipt is not a credit until **their** ledger shows it. Card corridors can look instant and still reverse days later as a chargeback — next lesson.

This door is dull. Dull is good. You are a customer of a company that already has your KYC, sending money down a pipe they published.

## 2. P2P inside a major platform

You pick an advertiser. You pay **their** personal or business bank details as the platform instructs. You mark “paid.” They release USDT into your **exchange** balance (still an IOU). The platform holds a dispute process if they cheat.

This is how a huge amount of local crypto on-ramping actually happens. It is also a scam factory. The lesson after next is only about surviving it. Hold this for now: in-app P2P still lands as an exchange IOU, not as BscScan.

## 3. Local brokers and WhatsApp desks

A person you know, or a “dealer.” You send local currency, they send USDT to an address. There is often **no** platform escrow. This is the highest trust requirement and the highest “the human vanished” rate. This academy does not romanticise it. If you use a person, you are doing an **OTC** trade — over-the-counter, a private deal — with no parent.

A better rate off-platform is often the price of no escrow.

TABLE
Door | Escrow? | Typical fail | Where the money sits if it “works”
Platform local currency / card / bank deposit | Company process | Name mismatch, delay, rejected deposit | CEX IOU
In-app P2P | Platform dispute | Fake receipt, delayed release, off-platform chat | CEX IOU
WhatsApp broker | Usually none | They take the local currency and disappear; or they send on the wrong network | Maybe coins on some chain, maybe nothing
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student pays a broker on WhatsApp because the rate is 15 local currency better. Broker asks for the USDT address.

1. The student, trying to be advanced, pastes a Trust Wallet BEP-20 address. Trust Wallet is an example of a wallet app, not an endorsement.
2. Broker sends USDT **TRC-20** on Tron “because fees are lower.”
3. The student sees nothing in Trust Wallet on BSC.
4. The broker says “it is confirmed, check Tronscan.” The local currency is gone. The coins exist on a chain the student was not watching.
5. Wrong book, again. A better rate bought a missing explorer row.

DIAGRAM
Your local money (local currency, dollars, euros, ...)
    |
    +--> official platform rails --> credited IOU
    +--> in-app P2P --> credited IOU (if release happens)
    +--> off-platform human --> maybe coins, maybe lesson in pain
    |
    v
Still not BNB Smart Chain until a withdrawal (or a broker send) hits YOUR address on that chain
ENDDIAGRAM

## Match names and amounts

Send the exact amount the advert or invoice says. Do not add “for food” in the bank narration if the advert says not to. Do not round up to a lucky number. Bots and humans who want a dispute handle will use any mismatch.

Send from an account in **your** name, the name that matches KYC. A cousin’s transfer is a freeze waiting for a Monday.

In countries where the exchange takes cards or local bank rails, still read the name on the beneficiary. Corporate account of the platform is one thing. A personal account pasted in chat is another.

## Rates are not this course

This course will not give you a current local currency rate, a named broker, or a “best advert.” Rates move. People who DM rates into your academy chat are selling. Compare inside a platform you chose on purpose, on a calm day.

USDT is not “the dollar in your pocket.” It is a token brand that tracks a dollar by issuer promise, on several chains. The local currency (or local currency-to-dollar) conversion is a local market. Do not treat a Twitter screenshot as a central-bank print.

NOTE
This academy will not quote a rate, name a broker, or tell you to buy Crystal Stones with the local currency that just became an IOU. When paid tracks go live, tuition is USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout — not a chat desk, not PaynovaX, not a personal account.
ENDNOTE

## Other countries, same sentence

A learner in London might use Faster Payments. A learner in the euro area might use SEPA. A learner in the US might use ACH or a card. A learner in Lagos might use P2P local currency. The plumbing changes. The sentence does not: **national currency became a company row, not a BscScan row.**

If your corridor is a local fintech wallet that then “buys USDT,” read whether you now have a fintech IOU, a CEX IOU, or an on-chain token. Three different bosses. The fintech app saying “USDT” without a network picker is usually still their ledger.

Do not skip this identification because the icon is green. Icons are not books.

## What this lesson is for

You should be able to point at any funding story and say which door it is, whether escrow exists, and which book the credit will sit on if it works.

## Say this out loud

- Naira — or any local currency — never sits on BNB Smart Chain. A door converts it into an IOU or into coins.
- In-app P2P has a dispute process. WhatsApp usually does not.
- Name mismatch is how freezes start. Exact amount, exact name.
- A better rate off-platform is often the price of no escrow.
- A credited exchange balance is still not a BscScan row.

Next: bank and card corridors — delays, chargebacks, and why “paid” is not “settled.”

lessons.title: Bank / card corridors, delays, and chargebacks
lessons.content:
# Bank / card corridors, delays, and chargebacks

Not every country lives on P2P. Many learners will fund an exchange through a **bank transfer** or a **card**. Those rails have parents. Parents can delay you, freeze you, and sometimes reverse you.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what a corridor is, why a receipt is not settlement, what a **chargeback** does to a crypto IOU, and why paying from someone else’s card is how accounts die. **Corridor** means: a permitted pipe between a national-currency system and a company’s ledger.

## Bank transfers are messages between ledgers

When you send local currency to an exchange’s corporate account, or dollars by ACH, or euros by SEPA, you are asking two banks (and sometimes a chain of correspondent banks) to rewrite books. Crypto is not in that sentence yet.

What can go wrong:

- **Name mismatch.** The sending account is not the KYC name. Compliance holds the deposit.
- **Reference / memo missing.** Some platforms need a code in the narration so they can attach the money to you. Next lesson treats memos on crypto deposits; fiat deposits have the same shape.
- **Weekend and cut-off times.** “I sent it” on Saturday is not “they have it” on Saturday.
- **Limits.** First-day caps, monthly caps, enhanced due diligence after a round number.

A bank SMS that says “debit successful” means your bank reduced your row. It does not mean the exchange credited you.

## Cards feel instant and stay reversible

Card networks often allow a **chargeback**: the cardholder disputes a payment and the scheme may pull the money back. That protects shoppers. It also means:

- the exchange may delay withdrawals until the card payment is less likely to reverse
- if you chargeback after spending the IOU, the company will freeze you and possibly more
- “buy crypto with a credit card and cash out” is a how-to for fraud teams, not a life hack

If you fund with a card, assume withdrawals are sticky for a while. That delay is the company not wanting to be the exit node of a chargeback.

TABLE
Rail | Feels like | Reversal risk | Typical beginner fail
Local bank transfer to platform | Hours to days | Lower than cards, not zero | Wrong name, missing reference, weekend
International wire | Days | Recovery is legal, not a button | Correspondent fees, SWIFT delays, compliance
Card | Seconds | Chargeback window | Instant buy, instant withdraw, then freeze
App-to-app fintech | Minutes | Depends on the fintech’s partner banks | Paying from an account not in your KYC name
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Marta, outside Nigeria, funds an example CEX with a debit card for the equivalent of 200 USDT.

1. The card shows a hold immediately. The exchange shows a credit.
2. She market-buys USDT and tries to withdraw the same hour to a BSC address.
3. The exchange blocks the withdrawal: “risk review, card purchases withdrawable after X days.”
4. She calls it a scam. It is a chargeback window. The company is not her enemy for keeping the IOU un-withdrawable until the card rail is colder.
5. If she instead files a chargeback “because crypto is slow,” she may lose the account and still owe the company.

DIAGRAM
Bank or card  -->  your bank / scheme ledger
        |
        v
Clearing (hours, days, or a card hold)
        |
        v
Exchange credits an IOU  (or holds it pending)
        |
        v
Withdrawals may wait until reversal risk drops
ENDDIAGRAM

## Do not mix names, do not “borrow a card”

Paying from a partner’s card, a business account that is not on the KYC file, or a friend’s fintech app is how you look like a mule. Even if you are innocent, the pattern is the pattern risk engines score.

If the platform publishes a corporate beneficiary, use it. If a chat says “our bank is down, pay this personal account,” you have left the corridor and entered OTC.

In Nigeria, some people bounce between bank transfer into a P2P seller and a platform NGN wallet. Those are still two doors. Read which book credited you. A NGN wallet on the exchange is local-currency IOU, not USDT, not BNB.

## Delays are not always theft

Honest delays: weekends, first-deposit reviews, extra selfies, travel-rule fields, bank holidays in another country. Dishonest delays: a WhatsApp desk that has your local currency and no coins. Distinguish by **where you paid**. Official beneficiary plus a ticket is a queue. Personal account plus silence is a problem.

NOTE
This academy does not tell you to chargeback an exchange because a candle moved. Chargebacks on crypto buys are how people get banned and, in some places, investigated. If you cannot afford the practice size without clawing it back from a card scheme, the size is too large.
ENDNOTE

## What to do while you wait

Waiting is when people invent side doors. They pay a cousin’s account. They accept a WhatsApp rate. They file a chargeback because Saturday felt long.

While you wait: keep the bank receipt, keep the exchange deposit ID, do not send a second payment, do not let a DM “speed it up” for a fee. If Monday still shows nothing, ticket on the bookmark with those IDs. Banks also have investigation windows. Parallel DMs do not shorten them.

If your card issuer already reversed a crypto purchase you actually received as IOU, expect the CEX to claw the IOU or ban the account. You cannot keep both the USDT and the reversed local currency. That is not a glitch. That is the rail.

## What this lesson is for

You should fund through a pipe you can explain, wait for their ledger — not your bank SMS — and not treat a card credit as instantly withdrawable coins.

## Say this out loud

- A corridor is a permitted pipe from national currency into a company book.
- Debit SMS is not an exchange credit. Exchange credit is not yet on-chain.
- Cards can reverse. Companies delay withdrawals for that reason.
- Pay from the name on the KYC file. Borrowed cards look like mule flow.
- Official slow rails beat unofficial fast personal accounts.

Next: P2P without becoming the victim — escrow, release, and why off-platform chat is the hole.

lessons.title: P2P without becoming the victim (escrow, release, off-platform chat)
lessons.content:
# P2P without becoming the victim (escrow, release, off-platform chat)

**P2P** means you trade with another person. The platform is supposed to **escrow** the crypto — lock it — until you pay, then **release** when both sides behave. Scammers attack the gaps.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to run a dull P2P buy or refuse a thrilling one, and you should treat “release before the goods” as a sentence that empties people. This is defensive. It is not a complete catalogue of every con. It is the patterns that empty beginners.

## Rule 0 — stay on the platform

The moment someone says “Bank is down, let’s finish on WhatsApp, I will send first,” escrow is gone. Decline. Report. Find another advert.

Off-platform chat is how they delete the recording, send new bank details, and recruit you into a second payment. The trade UI is the parent. Private chat is the hole.

## Fake receipts (you are selling)

You are **selling** USDT (they pay local currency into your bank). They send a Photoshop transfer receipt. Your bank has not credited you. They pressure you to release because “I have a plane.”

**Release only when the money is in your account, under your name, and you understand whether that credit can reverse.** Instant alerts can still reverse in some rails. Know your bank. If you do not know, wait. A PDF is not a credit. A credit may still bounce. “Release before goods” — here the goods are final local currency — is how sellers get emptied.

## You are buying USDT — they say they paid

The opposite direction. You send local currency to the seller’s bank details shown **in the app**. You mark paid. They stall. Open a dispute **in the app** with your real bank proof. Do not send a second payment. Do not take the argument to Telegram.

If they send a hash “I already sent USDT on-chain,” you are not even in a CEX P2P any more. Check nothing in panic. The escrowed IOU is the object. On-chain theatre is a distraction.

## Wrong-name payments

Someone pays you from an account that is not the name in the P2P profile. That can be a stolen bank account. If you release, the real owner later reverses or files a police case and **you** look like the exit node. Cancel / dispute. Do not “just this once.”

## Overpayment and refund theatre

They “accidentally” send more and ask you to refund the extra off-platform. The original payment later bounces. You refunded real money. Classic.

## Chargeback after release

On some payment methods the local currency can be clawed back after you released USDT. This is why experienced P2P sellers restrict methods. As a beginner **buyer**, prefer methods the platform ranks as robust, even if the rate is slightly worse.

TABLE
Pressure line | Translation
“Release I have an emergency” | They want escrow gone before your bank is final
“Let’s go to WhatsApp” | They want no recording
“Pay an extra 2,000 for the agent” | New invoice, not in the trade
“Send to this other account, that one is down” | Off-script bank details
“I sent USDT already, here is a hash” | Could be a different chain, a different token, or a lie — check nothing; use the trade UI
“Release first, I am a verified merchant” | Verified is a badge, not final local currency
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Blessing buys 100 USDT. Seller’s in-app account is Aisha.

1. Blessing’s bank transfer goes to Aisha as shown in the trade, exact amount, from Blessing’s own account.
2. She waits for her debit to show, marks paid, uploads the receipt **in the trade**.
3. Seller delays 20 minutes. Blessing does not send a second transfer. She does not move to WhatsApp.
4. She waits the timer and opens dispute.
5. The platform releases after seeing a matching bank debit. Boring. Correct.

If instead she had accepted new bank details in chat, she would be arguing with a ghost.

DIAGRAM
In-app trade open (crypto escrowed)
    |
    v
Pay EXACT details shown in the trade
    |
    v
Mark paid + proof in the trade
    |
    v
Wait for release or dispute in the app
    |
    X  never follow new details in private chat
    X  never release because a PDF arrived
ENDDIAGRAM

## Reputation is a clue, not a guarantee

Completion rate, badge, “merchant.” Useful. Not a parent. A high-volume advertiser can still send a fake receipt on a busy night. Your rule is the bank book and the trade UI, not the badge.

If you are new, start tiny. A first P2P is a procedure test, not a salary conversion.

NOTE
If a trade feels like a thriller, you are being played. Real P2P is dull: exact amount, exact name, wait, release. Adrenaline is a signal to stop. This academy will not match you with a seller and will not tell you to release early as a favour.
ENDNOTE

## Buying versus selling are different jobs

As a **buyer** of USDT, your job is: exact details in the trade, one payment, proof in the trade, wait or dispute. You are trying not to pay twice and not to follow new accounts.

As a **seller** of USDT, your job is stricter: escrow is your friend, release is irreversible on the crypto side, PDFs are nothing, wrong-name local currency is toxic, “release I have a plane” is a script. If you are new, prefer buying a tiny amount to learn the UI before you sell anything.

This academy is not training you to be a P2P desk. One practice buy is enough. Becoming a merchant is a business with police-report tails when a stolen bank account hits you. Stay small.

## What this lesson is for

You should be able to complete a small in-app P2P without following a human off the rails, and you should never release on a picture of money.

## Say this out loud

- Stay in the trade UI. Chat off-platform is a red flag.
- Receipts are not credits. Credits may still reverse — know your rail.
- Do not release before the goods: final money in your named account.
- Wrong-name money is toxic. Never pay twice. Dispute once.
- A hash in chat is not the escrowed IOU.

Next: stablecoins arriving from another chain — still the wrong book if you pick wrong.

lessons.title: Stablecoins arriving from another chain — still the wrong book if you pick wrong
lessons.content:
# Stablecoins arriving from another chain — still the wrong book if you pick wrong

USDT is a **brand** on several books. Depositing it onto an exchange is the same trap as withdrawing it, run in reverse.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to read a deposit screen, match asset plus network plus address plus memo if any, and refuse the belief that “USDT is one chain.” A **deposit address** is an address the exchange gave you for one asset on one network. It is not a universal USDT bucket.

## The deposit screen is a filter, not a suggestion

When you tap Deposit USDT, the platform asks for a **network**. That choice mint a (or reveals a) deposit address for **that** book.

- **BEP-20 / BSC** — BNB Smart Chain. Address looks like `0x…`. This academy’s practice rail.
- **ERC-20** — Ethereum. Also `0x…`. Different book. Gas in ETH.
- **TRC-20** — Tron. Often `T…`. Different book entirely.
- Others: Solana, Arbitrum, Polygon, “omnichain” labels that beginners should not improvise with.

If you send BEP-20 USDT to a TRC-20 deposit address, you did not “almost get it right.” You wrote in the wrong notebook. Recovery, if any, is a support ticket plus a maybe. Small stacks often die there.

The `0x` shape is the trap between BEP-20 and ERC-20. Same text family. Not the same money.

TABLE
You send | Exchange deposit set to | Result
USDT BEP-20 | USDT-BEP20 | Credit, after their confirmations
USDT BEP-20 | USDT-ERC20 (0x address on Ethereum) | Wrong book; ticket territory
USDT TRC-20 | USDT-BEP20 | Wrong book
USDT ERC-20 | USDT-ERC20 | Credit, often slower and costlier
BNB (native) | USDT deposit address | Wrong asset, even on the same chain
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Efe has USDT on Tron in an old wallet from a previous year. He wants it on an example CEX to convert, then later withdraw on BSC.

1. He opens Deposit, asset USDT, and leaves the default network. The default is TRC-20 this week.
2. He actually copies a BEP-20 address from a different screen because it looked like his wallet’s `0x`.
3. He sends TRC-20 USDT to an `0x` BSC deposit. The Tron explorer shows success. The exchange shows 0.
4. Support may or may not recover. A test send would have cost a few dollars and revealed the mismatch.
5. “USDT is USDT” was the false sentence. USDT is a name on several books.

DIAGRAM
Sender wallet network  ----must match----  Exchange deposit network
        |                                      |
        v                                      v
   tx on that chain                    credit on their IOU book

If the arrows point at different chains, the IOU never appears.
The explorer of the SENDING chain will still say success.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Credits take confirmations, not feelings

Exchanges wait for a number of **confirmations** — extra pages of the book on top of your transaction — before they credit you. That is their risk policy, not a bug. BNB Smart Chain is usually faster than Ethereum. “It’s been ten minutes” is not an argument. Paste the hash into the explorer **for the network you sent on**, then wait their counter.

Do not send a second deposit “to push it.” If the first was wrong-network, the second can be wrong twice.

## Incoming from a friend or a broker

If someone else sends USDT to your exchange deposit, you still pick the network they will actually use, and you still give them the address for **that** network. Read it back: asset, network, first 6 and last 6 of the address, memo if the screen shows one.

A broker who “always sends TRC-20” is not compatible with your BSC-only plan unless you accept a Tron deposit and later convert. Do not mix by accident.

Crystal Stones as a BEP-20 — contract `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` to verify only — is not USDT. Depositing it to a USDT address is the wrong asset. This academy still will not tell you to buy or deposit it.

NOTE
If a deposit does not credit, stop. Copy the tx hash. Open the explorer for the network you used. Compare to the network the deposit screen named. Then open a ticket on the bookmarked app. Do not hire a recovery agent who wants a seed. There is no seed on an exchange deposit; they are fishing.
ENDNOTE

## “USDT0”, bridges, and other labels you should not improvise with

Newer names — bridged USDT, “canonical” USDT, USDT on side-systems — will keep appearing. A beginner rule that survives the new labels: **if you did not choose that exact name on both sides of the send, do not send.**

Bridges are their own companies or contracts, with their own failure modes. This course does not teach bridging. If a desk says “send any USDT, we convert,” they are asking you to trust a private conversion. That is an OTC promise, not a network feature.

Test sends are cheaper than a support essay about a bridge you did not mean to use. If the deposit page lists five USDT flavours, pick one with your finger and say it out loud: “BEP-20 USDT to this 0x on BSC.” Then send that, tiny first.

## What this lesson is for

You should treat every inbound stablecoin as asset-plus-network, test-sized, and you should never believe USDT is a single chain.

## Say this out loud

- USDT is a brand on several books. BEP-20, ERC-20, and TRC-20 are not interchangeable.
- The deposit network must match the sending wallet’s network.
- Explorer success on the sending chain is not an exchange credit.
- Do not send a second stack to “push” a missing credit.
- Wrong asset (BNB into USDT, Crystal Stones into USDT) is also a wrong book.

Next: deposit memos and tags — why a missing memo is not “the blockchain ate it.”

lessons.title: Deposit memos, tags, and why a missing memo is not “the blockchain ate it”
lessons.content:
# Deposit memos, tags, and why a missing memo is not “the blockchain ate it”

Some deposits need more than an address. They need a **memo**, **tag**, **comment**, or **destination tag**: an extra number or string that tells a company whose IOU to credit, because many customers share one on-chain address.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to see a memo field and treat it as required, explain why the chain can confirm a transfer that the exchange still has not credited, and refuse the folklore that “the blockchain ate it.” **Memo** here does not mean a note to self. It is routing data for a pooled address.

## Why companies use memos

On some networks (historically XRP, XLM, some EOS-like designs, and various exchange-specific setups), one hot wallet receives thousands of deposits. The **address** is the company’s. The **memo** is you.

If you send to the right address with no memo, the coins arrived — at the company — and they do not know which row to increment. The book of the chain is fine. Their customer database is stuck. That is a support ticket, not a vanished transaction.

BNB Smart Chain USDT deposits to a personal-looking `0x` address often do **not** use a memo. Do not invent one. Do not skip one when the screen shows the field as required. Read the screen you have, not a memory of a different coin.

TABLE
What you did | Chain explorer | Exchange ledger
Right address, right network, memo correct (or not required) | Confirmed | Credit after their confirmations
Right address, right network, memo missing when required | Confirmed | No credit until they identify you — if they can
Wrong network | Confirmed on the wrong book | No credit
Memo present but for the wrong person | Confirmed | Maybe credited to someone else; ticket
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Kunle deposits an asset that shows Address plus Memo on his example CEX.

1. He copies the address carefully. He skips the memo because “I never needed one for USDT on BSC.”
2. The sending wallet confirms. The explorer of that chain shows success. He tweets that the blockchain ate his money.
3. The chain did its job. The company received coins into a pooled wallet with no customer tag.
4. He opens a ticket on the bookmarked app, pastes the tx hash, his user ID, the amount, and the time. He does not send a seed. There is no seed.
5. Recovery, if the firm offers it, can take days and sometimes a fee. A test send with the memo would have been cheaper.

DIAGRAM
Your wallet
    |
    v
On-chain tx to COMPANY address  (+ memo/tag if the screen required it)
    |
    v
Company software reads memo  -->  credits YOUR IOU
    |
    X  missing memo --> coins at company, no row for you yet
ENDDIAGRAM

## Memos are not optional when the screen says they are not

“Optional” on some wallets means the wallet will let you broadcast without one. The exchange still needs it. Optional in the sending UI is not optional in the receiving company.

Copy memo with the copy button. Check a few characters. Do not type a memo from memory in a chat. Do not use last week’s memo if you generated a new deposit. Some platforms rotate tags.

If the deposit screen says “no memo required,” do not paste a random number “for safety.” Extra data can break a simple transfer.

## This is not a Crystal Stones BEP-20 thing by default

Crystal Stones on BNB Smart Chain is a BEP-20 at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` (verify only). Ordinary BEP-20 transfers to an `0x` address do not use XRP-style memos. If a stranger says “send Crystal Stones with memo 1234 to unlock listing,” they are inventing a rail. Academy checkout, when live, is USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) through academy checkout — follow **that** screen’s fields, not a chat memo.

## How to talk to support when a memo was missing

Stay on the bookmarked app. Provide:

- tx hash
- amount and asset
- network you used
- timestamp
- screenshot of the deposit page (not of a seed, not of 2FA)

Never send a seed. An exchange problem has no seed. Anyone who says they need it to “find the memo on-chain” is a thief.

NOTE
A missing memo is a labelling failure at the company, not a hole in BNB Smart Chain physics. Stop. Ticket. Do not send a second full-size deposit as a poke. Test sends exist so the first mistake is small.
ENDNOTE

## Destination tags versus payment comments versus narrations

Three different “notes” get mixed:

- **Chain memo / tag / destination tag** — load-bearing for pooled crypto deposits.
- **Bank narration** — load-bearing for some fiat deposits; some P2P adverts forbid certain words.
- **Chat comment** — not load-bearing. A WhatsApp “memo: 44521” does not attach a chain memo.

If the CEX deposit screen shows a memo field, that is category one. Copy it. If a P2P advert says “do not write crypto in the bank narration,” that is category two. If a stranger sends a memo in chat for a BEP-20 USDT send that the official screen said needed no memo, that is category three — ignore it.

Mixing the three is how people put a bank story on a chain send and then blame BscScan.

## What this lesson is for

You should read every extra field on a deposit screen as possibly load-bearing, and you should describe a missing credit without blaming “the blockchain” when an explorer already shows the tx.

## Say this out loud

- A memo or tag routes a deposit into your IOU when many customers share one address.
- If the screen requires a memo, it is not optional even if the sending wallet allows a skip.
- Explorer confirmed plus exchange zero often means labelling, wrong network, or waiting on confirmations — not “the blockchain ate it.”
- Do not invent memos on ordinary BEP-20 USDT if the screen says none is required.
- Support gets a hash and a ticket, never a seed.

Take the quiz. Next module: a first spot buy, sized like an adult — including why you need BNB even if you bought USDT.

lessons.title: Market, limit, and a practice size
lessons.content:
# Market, limit, and a practice size

You have a local currency-credited IOU, or a card-credited IOU, or you already hold USDT on the exchange. You want a little BNB, or you want to convert something. The two beginner buttons are **market** and **limit**. The third, unspoken button is **size**.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what each order type does, pick a practice size that does not change rent, and refuse the idea that clicking Buy made you a trader. **Practice size** means: an amount you can lose to a mistake — wrong network, fat-finger, a freeze — without missing rent, fees, or food.

## Market

“Take the current ask (when buying) and just do it.” Fast. You pay the spread. On liquid pairs (BNB/USDT on a major CEX) this is how a first **small** buy should look. You are not trying to save 0.02%. You are trying to not miss-click.

A market order is usually a **taker** order: you hit resting liquidity. You will pay the taker fee. On a deep book that fee plus a tiny spread is the cost of being done.

On a thin book a market order **is** the candle. You can buy the next 3% of the book by yourself. If you cannot explain the 24-hour volume, you should not market-buy that pair.

## Limit

“I will buy if the price reaches X.” Your order sits on the book as a **maker** (if it rests) until someone hits it — or it does not fill. Beginners leave limit orders and then also market-buy, doubling the position, then panic.

Limits are how you avoid paying a silly ask on a jumpy pair. They are also how you forget an order exists. For this course: **market on a liquid pair, tiny size**, unless you already understand why you are placing a limit, and you will check Open Orders before you do anything else.

**Stop** and **OCO** (one-cancels-the-other) are extra machinery. Walk past them until spot plus size is boring.

## Size: practise with amounts you can lose

Define **practice** before you click:

- an amount that does not change rent
- an amount you can afford to mis-send on a wrong network once (you will try not to)
- not a month of salary “because the group said it will 10x”
- not borrowed money, not a credit-card float you plan to chargeback

If the number makes your hands shake, it is too large for a first buy. Shrink it. There is no prize for a large first fill.

This academy’s success metric is: you can narrate what you bought, what you paid in fees, and what still sits as an IOU. It is not: you caught a wick.

TABLE
Move | Beginner default | Not this course
First conversion into USDT | Small, liquid, on-platform | Salary-sized “because the rate is good today”
First BNB for gas | Small; you need it later to move tokens | All-in on BNB as a trade
First withdrawal | Even smaller test, then the rest | The whole stack on an untested address
First thin alt / “Crystal Stones on a random book” | Not in this course | Ape because the ticker matches
Futures / 100x | Closed door | “Just a small leverage”
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Emeka funds 30,000 local currency as practice.

1. He buys USDT on a liquid door — P2P or the platform’s listed pair — at a size that is not rent.
2. He market-buys a slice of BNB so a later wallet will have gas. Liquid pair. Tiny.
3. He does not hunt a 40x ticker the same evening. He does not open futures “just to see.”
4. He will withdraw a test in the next module. He still has rent.
5. That is a successful first buy even if the local currency rate moved against him by 1%. The skill was the checklist, not the candle.

DIAGRAM
Liquid pair + market + small size  -->  boring fill --> IOU you can explain
Thin pair + market + pride         -->  you are the candle
Limit + forgotten open order       -->  surprise second fill
Hands shaking                      -->  shrink the size; do not “be brave”
ENDDIAGRAM

## Slippage and fat-finger

**Slippage** is the difference between the price you glanced at and the price you got. On BNB/USDT spot on a major CEX, usually tiny. On a low-liquidity token, a market buy can print a ridiculous candle **you** made.

Fat-finger is the extra zero. Read the notional — “you will spend 20 USDT,” not “you will spend 200.” Some screens confirm in quote asset, some in base. Read both. If the confirm popup is a surprise, cancel.

Do not ape the next ticker. Stop rules live in a later lesson this module. Today’s rule is smaller: if you cannot name the pair, the size, and the fee line, you do not click.

NOTE
This academy will not tell you to buy Crystal Stones, BNB, or USDT as an investment. BNB here is fuel you may need later on BNB Smart Chain. USDT is a practice stablecoin brand. Size is a safety tool. Education only.
ENDNOTE

## Min notional, lots, and the “cannot place order” popup

If the platform rejects a 2 USDT buy, you may be under **minimum notional**. That is a house rule. Raise to the minimum if and only if the minimum is still practice money. If the minimum is no longer practice, that pair is not your first buy. Pick a more liquid pair with a smaller door, or wait.

Some pairs trade in awkward lot sizes. The confirm popup is where you catch “I wanted 10 USDT of BNB and I am about to spend 10 BNB.” Read the unit. Cancel is a skill.

Practice size also means: no adding funds mid-fill because a candle moved. The ticket you defined before the click is the ticket.

## What this lesson is for

You should leave this page able to place a tiny market buy on a liquid spot pair and know that you still hold an IOU, not a personality as a trader.

## Say this out loud

- Market on a liquid pair is the beginner default. You pay spread plus taker fee to be done.
- Limit orders are optional; they are how people double-fill if they forget Open Orders.
- If the size scares you, shrink it. Practice means you can lose it.
- You are not yet a trader because you clicked Buy.
- Thin books plus market orders make you the candle.

Next: the BNB problem — why you need BNB even if you bought USDT.

lessons.title: Why you need BNB even if you bought USDT
lessons.content:
# Why you need BNB even if you bought USDT

On BNB Smart Chain, **BNB pays gas**. USDT does not. Crystal Stones does not. A wallet full of tokens and 0 BNB is a display case you cannot open.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what native coin versus token means on BSC, why withdrawing USDT alone can strand you, and how you will get a little BNB without handing a seed to a “gas helper.” **Gas** means: the fee the network charges to include your signed instruction in the public book. On BSC that fee is paid in BNB.

## Two layers on the same address

Your `0x` address on BSC can hold:

- **BNB** — native coin, used for fees. Sending BNB is a simple value transfer.
- **BEP-20 tokens** — USDT, Crystal Stones, everything else that is a **contract**. Spending a token means: sign a transaction, pay gas in BNB, the contract updates balances.

No BNB, no send, no approve, no swap. The tokens are still on the book. You are looking through glass.

This is not unique to BSC. Ethereum needs ETH. Tron has a different energy/bandwidth design. Solana needs SOL. The beginner pattern is always: the native coin is fuel; the stablecoin is cargo.

## The stranded-USDT pattern

1. User withdraws **only** USDT from the exchange, network BEP-20, to Trust Wallet (an example of a wallet app).
2. They later want to send some to a friend, to the checkout processor, or to a dApp.
3. Wallet says insufficient funds for gas.
4. They google. A helper says “send me the seed, I will add gas.”
5. You already know how that ends. The helper adds nothing. They empty the USDT — if they can trick you into a signature or a seed — or they vanish with a “gas fee” you prepaid.

The fix is boring: when you withdraw, include a **small BNB** withdrawal too — more than one future transaction, less than a trophy. Same address, network BNB Smart Chain / BNB native, not a random BEP-20 named BNB.

TABLE
You hold on BSC | Can you send it without BNB?
BNB | Yes (BNB pays for its own send)
USDT (BEP-20) | No
Crystal Stones (BEP-20) | No
A random airdrop token | No — and you often should not try
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Maya withdraws 40 USDT and 0.02 BNB to the same address.

1. Weeks later she moves 10 USDT. Gas is a fraction of that BNB.
2. She still has gas for mistakes and for a second send.
3. She never needed a helper. She never pasted a seed. An exchange login was never a seed either.
4. If 0.02 BNB feels mysterious, she looks at current gas on a real tx on BscScan **before** she withdraws. She wants many ordinary transfers of headroom, not a scientific minimum that fails when the network is busy.
5. If she had withdrawn USDT only, she would now be shopping for BNB under panic, which is how “gas station” scams sell.

DIAGRAM
Exchange IOU
   |
   +--> USDT on BEP-20  -->  tokens in wallet (cargo)
   +--> BNB on BSC      -->  fuel to move those tokens
   |
   v
Later: the checkout processor USDT BEP-20 (academy checkout when live)
still needs BNB in the sending wallet to pay gas
ENDDIAGRAM

## Do not pay gas to a stranger address

Scams: “gas station” sites that ask for a seed, or that take USDT and never send BNB. If you need BNB, withdraw BNB from the **same** exchange you already use, to **your** address, or swap a tiny amount on a venue you already trust. Do not discover a new website on the day you are stranded.

Do not send USDT to a Telegram “I’ll swap you BNB.” That is P2P without escrow, under panic. Panic is their leverage.

PancakeSwap is a DEX you are not using yet. Do not connect a wallet to a clone swap to “turn USDT into BNB” on the night you are stuck. That is how approvals drain you. Come back in Intermediate with a calm brain.

## How much BNB is “a little”

Enough for many simple token transfers, not a trading inventory. Amounts change with network conditions. Look at a few ordinary BscScan token transfers, read the BNB fee, multiply by a conservative number (tens of transfers, not two). Then add slack. Dust-level BNB that cannot pay one send is not fuel. It is a decoration.

NOTE
Academy checkout for paid tracks later expects USDT on BNB Smart Chain. It still will not pay your gas for you. Keeping a little BNB is part of living on BSC. We will not tell you to buy BNB as an investment. We will tell you that tokens do not pay their own fare.
ENDNOTE

## Paying academy checkout later, still needs fuel

When Intermediate checkout is live, you will send USDT on BEP-20 to the checkout processor through a published page. That send is an on-chain token transfer. It will not go through if the sending wallet has USDT and 0 BNB.

So the “little BNB” is not a trading opinion. It is fare for later adult payments, including tuition, including sending to a friend, including moving to a new device’s address. Buy it as a tiny spot conversion on the CEX, withdraw it as native BNB on BSC, keep it as fuel. Do not farm it through a stranger’s gas station.

If BNB’s local currency price scares you, you need less BNB, not zero BNB. Look at fees on BscScan, multiply, add slack. Fear of the fuel price is how people skip fuel and then panic.

## What this lesson is for

You should never withdraw a token-only stack to BSC and call the job done. Fuel is part of the first buy.

## Say this out loud

- BNB is fuel on BNB Smart Chain. Tokens are cargo. USDT does not pay gas.
- Withdrawing USDT alone can strand you looking at a balance you cannot move.
- A helper who adds gas in exchange for a seed is a thief.
- Withdraw a little BNB on purpose, same address, native BNB on BSC.
- Panic gas stations and clone DEX sites are how stranded people get emptied.

Next: a full first-buy walkthrough, as a story you can copy as a checklist — not as a command to buy today.

lessons.content:
# Walkthrough: a boring first buy (narrated, not a call to action)

This lesson stitches the course so far into one narrative. It is **education**. It is not an instruction to open an account this hour, not a rate quote, and not a buy order for Crystal Stones or any other token.

By the end you should be able to narrate Riley’s steps in your own words, including the step where Riley stops for the day. Meet Riley. Riley finished Crypto Foundations and Wallets. Riley wants a practice stack on BNB Smart Chain: USDT they control, plus BNB for gas. Riley can lose this amount without missing rent.

## 1. Decide the venue on a calm day

Riley picks a CEX that actually serves their country, using a bookmarked domain. Riley does not use a clone ad. Riley enables authenticator 2FA, sets an anti-phishing code, and does not photograph the 2FA QR into WhatsApp. Riley does not use SMS 2FA as the long-term lock. Binance, if Riley uses it, is an example of a centralised exchange, not a command.

Riley will later whitelist a withdrawal address. Not today, not a stranger’s address.

## 2. Fund

Riley uses in-app P2P, or a bank/card corridor if that exists in Riley’s country. Riley pays the **in-trade** or official beneficiary details, exact amount, own named account. Riley does not move to WhatsApp. USDT appears as an **exchange IOU**. Riley does not tweet a BscScan link. There is nothing to link yet.

If a card was used, Riley reads whether withdrawals are delayed. Riley does not rage at a chargeback window.

## 3. Keep a little BNB

Riley market-buys a small BNB amount against USDT on a liquid pair. Practice size. Riley does not spend the whole stack on a thin alt. Riley does not open futures. Riley checks the fee line on the receipt. Riley still holds IOUs.

## 4. Prepare the destination

Riley opens the **official** wallet app — Trust Wallet or MetaMask are examples of wallet apps, not endorsements — network **BNB Smart Chain**, copies the receive address by the wallet’s copy button. Riley does not type it by hand. Riley does not paste into a chat “please confirm this is right.” Clipboard malware is Module 5. Today Riley checks first 6 and last 6 on the wallet screen.

## 5. Withdrawal screen, read every line

- Asset: USDT
- Network: **BNB Smart Chain / BEP-20** (not ERC-20, not TRC-20, not a randomly named “BSC2”)
- Address: paste, visually check first 6 and last 6
- Amount: a **test** first
- Fee: visible

Riley sends the test. Riley opens BscScan, pastes **their** address, waits for the token transfer row. Only then Riley sends the rest, and a separate small BNB withdraw. If the test does not show, Riley stops. Riley does not send the rest to “push it.”

## 6. Whitelist and stop

After the test works, Riley whitelists that address for USDT and BNB. Future Riley is harder to steal. Riley does not then ape a ticker. Riley does not connect the wallet to a “claim Crystal Stones airdrop.” Riley does not screenshot the seed. Riley does not tell a group the exact amount.

TABLE
Step | Done when | Failure if skipped
Venue | Bookmark + authenticator 2FA + anti-phishing | Clone login
Fund | IOU visible; no off-platform side quest | WhatsApp broker, wrong name
BNB | Enough gas headroom bought as IOU, then withdrawn | Stranded USDT
Test withdraw | BscScan row on the right asset and network | Vanished stack
Rest + whitelist | Same address, same network | Stolen session later
Stop for the day | No airdrop, no thin alt, no futures | The night the group waited for
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** This whole lesson is the worked scenario. Numbered as Riley lived it:

1. Calm venue. Real domain. Authenticator. Anti-phishing word.
2. Fund via a parented door. Exact name. Exact amount. IOU, not chain.
3. Tiny BNB on a liquid spot market. Still IOUs.
4. Copy address from wallet on BNB Smart Chain. Eyes on first 6 and last 6.
5. Test USDT on BEP-20. Explorer agrees. Then the rest. Then BNB native.
6. Whitelist. Stop. Rent still exists. No Crystal Stones purchase. No the checkout processor practice to a chat wallet — tuition, when live, is a published checkout, not tonight’s improvisation.

DIAGRAM
Calm setup --> fund IOU --> slice of BNB --> test USDT on BEP-20
       --> explorer agrees --> remainder + BNB --> whitelist --> stop for the day

Any rush ("send now the window closes") --> abort
ENDDIAGRAM

## What Riley does not do that night

- does not connect the wallet to a DEX Riley is not using yet
- does not buy a clone token because the ticker is similar
- does not send Crystal Stones anywhere; Riley did not buy it, and this course did not ask Riley to
- does not pay a mentor who DMs a wallet
- does not skip the test because the fee “feels like a waste”

NOTE
If any step feels like a rush, abort. Liquidity will still exist tomorrow. Thieves prefer tonight. This walkthrough is a checklist you can speak. It is not a push notification to buy.
ENDNOTE

## Timing: this is not “tonight if the group is green”

Riley’s story is a sequence, not a clock. If KYC takes three days, the sequence waits. If a card corridor holds withdrawals for a week, the sequence waits. If the wallet seed is still in the camera roll, the sequence waits at the IOU.

Rushing the walkthrough to match a listing rumour is how step 5 (network radio) gets skipped. The walkthrough includes the word **stop**. If you cannot say stop, you are not narrating Riley. You are narrating the group.

Speak the walkthrough once without a phone in hand. Then, if you still want to practise with money you can lose, walk it slowly. This paragraph is still not a buy order.

## What this lesson is for

You should be able to teach Riley’s evening to someone else without turning it into a call to action or a branded advert.

## Say this out loud

- A first buy is a checklist, not a mood: venue, fund, BNB, test, explorer, rest, whitelist, stop.
- Test send, then the rest. Explorer agrees, or it did not happen.
- Exchange IOU and on-chain coins are different chapters of the same evening.
- Stop after the boring win. Do not ape, and do not buy Crystal Stones because a walkthrough existed.
- This was narration, not an order ticket.

Next: order books, slippage, and “filled” versus “I meant to.”

lessons.title: Order books, slippage, and “filled” versus “I meant to”
lessons.content:
# Order books, slippage, and “filled” versus “I meant to”

The button says Buy. The book decides what you get.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to glance at an order book, say what a fill is, name slippage without folklore, and refuse the sentence “I meant to buy at the last price.” An **order book** is the list of resting bids and asks at a venue: people willing to buy or sell at stated prices, in stated sizes.

## What the book is showing

Each **ask** is a sell order waiting. Each **bid** is a buy order waiting. Depth is how much size sits near the middle. A liquid pair has a thick book: many small steps. A thin pair has a cliff: one ask at 1.00 for dust, then 1.12 for more, then 1.40.

A **market buy** walks up the asks until your size is filled. Your average price is not the last trade and not the first ask. It is the weighted walk. That walk is **slippage** when it is worse than you glanced.

A **limit buy** at 1.00 sits until asks fall to you, or it sits forever. It will not chase. That is the feature. It is also why “I placed it” is not “I have the asset.”

## Filled, partial, cancelled, rejected

**Filled** means the venue matched you. You have a new IOU mix. The receipt is the truth, not the candle you wanted.

**Partial fill** means some size matched. The rest is still live or was cancelled depending on the order type. Beginners see 40% filled, buy again, then the rest fills. Double. Check Open Orders.

**Cancelled** means you or the system pulled it. **Rejected** means the engine said no: insufficient balance, trading halt, pair delisted, min notional too small.

“I meant to” is not a status. The book does not hear intent.

TABLE
You thought | Book did | Adult read
Last price was 600 | Your market buy ate asks up to 601.2 | Slippage on a liquid pair; usually small
Last price was 1.00 on a thin alt | Your market buy printed 1.18 | You were the candle
I placed a limit | Unfilled, still open | You do not have the asset yet
It filled twice | Residual plus a second market | You did not look at Open Orders
I bought Crystal Stones | You bought a ticker with a similar name | Contract not checked; this course still did not ask you to buy it
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Sam sees BNB/USDT last = 600. Sam market-buys a practice size.

1. The first ask is 600.1 for plenty of size. Sam fills at about 600.1 plus taker fee. Boring. Correct for this course.
2. Sam then “just looks” at a thin TOKEN/USDT book. Last is 0.050. Sam market-buys the same pride size.
3. The book had 20 USDT of asks near 0.050, then a gap. Sam’s average is 0.061. The chart prints a spike. The group says “whale.” The whale was Sam.
4. Sam did not get the last price. Sam got the walk. “I meant to buy at 0.050” is a diary entry, not a refund.
5. Sam checks the spot receipt, not Twitter. The fill is final on the company’s book.

DIAGRAM
Asks stacked above
   1.18  |||||
   1.12  |||
   1.00  |        <-- last trade was here, tiny
Bids stacked below
   0.92  |||
   0.90  |||||

A market buy of large size climbs the ask stairs.
The last trade was a footstep, not a floor.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Min notionals, tick size, and halt buttons

Exchanges set a **minimum notional** (you cannot buy 0.0001 USDT of something). They set a **tick size** (price increments). They can **halt** a pair. None of these are the chain. They are house rules. If a halt hits, your unfilled limit sits in limbo until they say otherwise. Your filled IOU is still their IOU.

PancakeSwap, a DEX you are not using yet, does not have this same book. It has a pool and a curve. Different machine. Do not import DEX folklore into a CEX ticket.

## How to not be surprised

- Read the confirm popup’s **estimated amount**
- Prefer liquid pairs for practice
- Cap size so a 1% walk is still practice money
- Look at Open Orders after every click
- Do not market-buy a thin book “because the screenshot was green”

NOTE
Filled is a venue fact. It is not a moral verdict and not a chain settlement. You still have not withdrawn. Education only — we are not coaching you to scalp spread or to hunt Crystal Stones wicks.
ENDNOTE

## Market orders on liquid pairs still deserve a glance at depth

Even BNB/USDT can gap around news. A one-second glance at the depth — is there size at this ask, or a paper-thin wall — is enough. If the wall is paper and your size is pride, switch to a limit you understand or shrink.

“Filled at a worse price than the YouTube thumbnail” is not refundable. Support will not unwind a spot fill because a candle looked different on another venue. The receipt is the venue’s truth.

If you placed a limit and it filled while you were asleep, that is the limit working. Check Open Orders and balances in the morning before you place another. Night fills plus morning markets is how size doubles without a second mood.

## Intent is not a status on the receipt

Support will not unwind a spot fill because a thumbnail on another venue looked cheaper. The receipt is this venue’s truth. If a limit filled while you slept, that is the limit working — check Open Orders before you place another, or size doubles without a second mood. “I meant to buy Crystal Stones” is the same grammar: intent is not a fill, and this course still did not ask for that fill.

## What this lesson is for

You should be able to look at a fill and describe it as a walk up (or down) a book, not as a broken promise from “the market.”

## Say this out loud

- The order book is resting bids and asks at one venue. Last is history.
- A market order walks the book. Slippage is that walk.
- Filled is what happened. “I meant to” is not a status.
- Partial fills plus a second click are how people double a position.
- Thin books are how a beginner becomes the candle.

Next: do not ape the next ticker — stop rules before the button.

lessons.title: Do not ape the next ticker — stop rules before the button
lessons.content:
# Do not ape the next ticker — stop rules before the button

The most expensive hour after a first buy is the hour you feel competent.

By the end of this lesson you should have a written **stop rule**: a sentence you say before any extra click, especially when a group drops a ticker. **Ape** means: buy because of urgency, shame, or a screenshot, without a size, a pair, or a reason you could repeat tomorrow. This academy will not tell you to buy Crystal Stones. It will tell you to stop.

## Competence is a mood, not a skill

You funded. You filled a liquid pair. You still hold IOUs. That is a procedure win. It is not a license to hunt 40x names. The brain treats “I did a thing in crypto” as “I should do more.” That is how practice size becomes rent.

Write the stop rules **before** you are in the chat. After is too late.

## Stop rules you can actually use

1. **One practice ticket per day.** Riley’s evening is enough. Sleep.
2. **No ticker you cannot spell and cannot find a contract for.** If it is Crystal Stones, the only contract this academy will ever name is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BNB Smart Chain, and naming it is verification, not a buy order.
3. **No futures, no leverage, no “copy trade.”** Spot only.
4. **No second asset because the first one “isn’t moving.”** Boredom is not a strategy.
5. **No size increase because you “understand it now.”** You understand a button. That is not alpha.
6. **If a message says “last chance,” it is not.** Liquidity, if real, will exist after you sleep. Thieves prefer tonight.

TABLE
Trigger | What you tell yourself | What you do
Group screenshot, green candle | Screenshots are not fills | Close the chat; book still closed
“Crystal Stones listing incoming” | Listing is a business claim to verify, not a market order | Do not buy; this course forbids the ape
Thin alt, 8% spread | I would be the candle | Walk away
Friends made money | They did not publish their all-in fees or the ones who lost | Your practice size stays practice
Boredom after a successful test withdraw | Competence mood | Stop for the day
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** After Riley’s boring first buy, a WhatsApp group posts “CSTN now, we go 10x, don’t miss.”

1. Riley wants to feel inside the room. Hands move toward Convert.
2. Riley reads the stop rules, out loud. One practice ticket per day. Already used.
3. Riley checks: is this even the contract `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`? The group paste is a different address with a similar name.
4. Riley buys nothing. Riley does not argue in the group. Arguing is how they keep you in the room until you click.
5. Next week some of the group is empty and asking for recovery agents. Riley still has the practice USDT and BNB. That is the win.

DIAGRAM
First boring fill
    |
    v
Competence mood  ----stop rules---->  go to sleep
    |
    X  ape the next ticker
    X  open futures "just to see"
    X  raise size because "I get it now"
    X  buy a clone contract with the right letters
ENDDIAGRAM

## What about “research”

Research, for this academy, is: which book, which contract, which fee, which size you can lose. It is not a ten-page PDF from the group. It is not a YouTuber’s leverage tutorial. If you cannot write four lines — asset, venue, size, what still sits as IOU — you are not researching. You are hunting a feeling.

Crystal Stones’ RWA story, if you meet it later, is **their claim to verify**. It is not a market order. It is not this lesson’s homework.

## The button is the last step, not the first

Before Buy:

- pair named, both sides
- spot, not futures
- size that does not change rent
- fee line visible
- stop rule still satisfied

If any line is missing, the button waits. The book will not send you a thank-you note for hesitating. Your future self might.

NOTE
This academy’s Basic track is not a trading desk. We will not celebrate a profitable ape. We will celebrate a student who can narrate a fill and then not take a second one. You should not buy Crystal Stones because you finished a walkthrough.
ENDNOTE

## Shame is a trading signal — for the other side

Groups use shame: “you still in USDT, coward.” Shame is not information about a book. It is social pressure toward a click. Your stop rules are allowed to sound boring in a loud chat. You do not owe the chat a conversion.

If you already aped once, the second rule is: do not ape-to-recover. The thin ticker that took 20% will not courteously give it back because you doubled. Practice size means you can close the app and still eat.

Write the rules on the same paper as the personal ledger. Rules that live only in a lesson file get forgotten at 11 p.m.

## Put the phone in another room

A stop rule can be physical: after the first fill, the phone leaves the room. Ridiculous. Effective. Shame from a group (“still in USDT, coward”) is not book information. If you already aped once, do not ape-to-recover. Practice size means you can close the app and still eat.

## What this lesson is for

You should have stop rules that survive a group chat, and you should treat “next ticker” as a test of those rules, not as opportunity.

## Say this out loud

- Competence after a first fill is a mood. It is not a reason to raise size.
- Stop rules are written before the chat, spoken before the button.
- Last-chance tickers, clone contracts, and futures buttons are how practice size dies.
- Naming Crystal Stones’ contract is verification, not a buy order.
- One boring ticket, then stop for the day.

Next: when the exchange screen and the chain will disagree — they should, because you have not withdrawn.

lessons.content:
# When the exchange screen and the chain will disagree (they should — you have not withdrawn)

After a spot buy, students open BscScan, paste an address, see zero, and panic. That panic is this lesson’s entire job.

By the end you should treat disagreement as the **expected** state until a withdrawal confirms, and you should know which screen is boss for which fact. **Boss screen** means: the ledger that is allowed to be right for that question.

## Two questions, two books

**Question A — What does the company owe me?**  
Boss: the exchange app, on the bookmarked site. Spot balances, open orders, funding history.

**Question B — What does BNB Smart Chain say my address holds?**  
Boss: BscScan (or your wallet talking to BSC). Only updates when an on-chain transaction hits that address.

If you have not withdrawn, BscScan **should** show 0 at your personal address (or whatever was already there from earlier). The exchange showing 50 USDT and BscScan showing 0 is not a bug. It is two honest books describing two different objects.

TABLE
Fact you want | Boss screen | Wrong screen
Available USDT IOU | Exchange spot wallet | BscScan
Open limit order | Exchange Open Orders | Your bank SMS
On-chain USDT at my 0x | BscScan token tab | Exchange screenshot
Whether a withdrawal left the company | Exchange withdrawal history plus explorer tx | A WhatsApp admin
BNB for gas on my address | BscScan + wallet on BSC | Exchange BNB IOU you have not withdrawn
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Riley has 40 USDT and 0.02 BNB as IOUs after the boring first buy. Riley has not withdrawn.

1. Riley pastes the Trust Wallet address into BscScan. Token tab: 0 USDT. BNB: 0.
2. A group member says “they stole it, the chain doesn’t see it.”
3. Riley says the sentence from Module 1: exchange balance is an IOU. The chain has never heard of Riley’s email.
4. Riley withdraws a test 1 USDT on BEP-20. After confirmations, BscScan shows 1 USDT. The exchange shows 39. Disagreement remains, smaller, and still correct.
5. Riley does not “fix” the remaining 39 by sending a seed to a helper who will “sync the chain.” There is nothing to sync. There is a withdrawal Riley has not clicked.

DIAGRAM
Exchange screen          BscScan at your 0x
   40 USDT IOU              0 USDT
   0.02 BNB IOU             0 BNB
        |                      ^
        |   only after withdraw |
        +----------------------+

Disagreement is the diagram.
Agreement happens per asset, per successful withdrawal.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Internal transfers and “I sent it to my other account”

If you move USDT from Spot to Funding, or to another user of the same CEX, BscScan still shows 0. You shuffled rows. If you send to a friend who uses a **different** company, that is usually a withdrawal (on-chain) or an off-platform mess. Read the screen: does it ask for a network? Then you are leaving the building.

## Explorers can also confuse you

BscScan will not show ERC-20 USDT. Etherscan will not show BEP-20 USDT. If you withdraw on BSC and search Etherscan, you will see 0 and think it failed. Wrong explorer is another disagreement that “should” happen.

Wallet apps hide tokens you have not “enabled.” The chain can hold a token the UI has not listed. BscScan token tab is the adult check, not a missing icon.

## When disagreement is actually a problem

- Withdrawal history says complete, explorer of **that** network shows nothing — wait confirmations, then ticket with hash.
- Explorer shows a tx to a different address — paste attack (Module 5).
- Explorer shows the tx on TRC-20 while you thought BEP-20 — wrong network.
- Exchange balance dropped with no withdrawal you started — session theft; freeze.

Those are problems. “I bought and BscScan is zero” is not, by itself.

NOTE
Do not let a helper “align the exchange with the chain” by taking remote control. The books are supposed to differ until you withdraw. Academy staff will not sync anything. the checkout processor checkout, when live, also will not show on your CEX screen; it will show on BscScan after you pay from a wallet that actually has USDT BEP-20 and BNB for gas.
ENDNOTE

## Screenshots are not either book

A screenshot of the CEX can be old. A screenshot of BscScan can be a different address. A screenshot from a group can be edited. When you reconcile, open the live bookmark and the live explorer. Do not reconcile against photos.

If a helper says “see, BscScan shows your USDT” and the URL is not bscscan.com on an address you recognise, you are being shown theatre. Type the explorer yourself. Paste the address yourself from the wallet receive screen.

Disagreement before withdraw is expected. Fake agreement from a stranger’s screenshot is an attack.

## Do not reconcile against photos, and do not use testnet

Open the live bookmark and the live explorer. A helper’s screenshot is theatre. Type bscscan.com yourself. Paste the address from the wallet receive screen. BSC testnet is a different book; practice money on mainnet (chain ID 56) will not appear there.

## What this lesson is for

You should hear “the screens disagree” and ask “have I withdrawn that asset on that network?” before you ask “was I robbed?”

## Say this out loud

- After a spot buy, the exchange screen and the chain should disagree. You have not withdrawn.
- Company book answers what they owe you. Explorer answers what your address holds.
- Internal transfers are still their ledger. No public hash.
- Wrong explorer (Etherscan for a BSC send) produces a fake zero.
- “Sync the chain” helpers are thieves. There is nothing to sync but a withdrawal you control.

Take the quiz. Next module: withdrawing without vanishing the stack — networks, test sends, paste attacks, explorers, dust and delays.
